entries.meaning: Marks a large but unspecified number of countable things.
examples: Many Americans commute more than an hour each way.
How many people are coming to dinner?
There aren't many seats left for the early show.
She has too many projects going at once.
Many of the applicants had never written a line of code.
The many delays finally cost the contractor the job.

body: Before a bare plural noun it names a big number drawn from an open set — many Americans, many companies. 2. After the, a possessive, or a demonstrative it is a postdeterminer and simply describes an already-identified set as a large one — the many problems we inherited. 3. As a pronoun it stands alone with no noun: Many were called, few were chosen.
examples: Many Americans commute more than an hour each way.
How many people are coming to dinner?
There aren't many seats left for the early show.
She has too many projects going at once.
Many of the applicants had never written a line of code.
The many delays finally cost the contractor the job.

entries.русский: много, многие — только с исчисляемыми во мн. ч.; с неисчисляемыми нужно much
entries.position: central when it opens the noun phrase (many people); postdeterminer after a central determiner (the many problems, her many friends, these many years)
entries.register: neutral — the standard written form; in plain affirmative speech Americans usually reach for a lot of
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — many people, many reasons, many times. Never an uncountable noun (✗ many information, ✗ many money, ✗ many advice — use much or a lot of) and never a singular countable noun (✗ many reason). The single exception is the fixed frame many a + singular noun, which has its own entry below.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — many of the students, many of my friends, many of them. Never ✗ many the students. No of before a bare plural: many students.
entries.pattern: many [plural countable] · many of [the/my/these + plural] · many of [them/us] · [the/her/these] many [plural] · how many [plural] · too / so / as many [plural] · many more [plural]
entries.contrast: Many counts, much measures: many books but much reading. Both are perfectly natural in questions and negatives (Do you have many?, There aren't many), and both sound stiff in a plain affirmative statement in American English, where a lot of is the spoken default — A lot of people came rather than Many people came, unless you are writing. Many stays comfortable in affirmatives when it is modified (so many, too many, as many, how many, many more) and throughout formal prose. Determiner against pronoun: many people left has a noun after it, many left does not.
entries.variants: so many, too many, as many, how many, many more, the many, a great many, a good many
entries.see also: much, more, a lot of, a great many, quite a few, few, how many

entries.meaning: Names a large number of countable things while treating them grammatically one at a time. The singular is the whole point: it makes the reader picture the cases individually rather than as a crowd, which is why the phrase sounds weighty and old-fashioned.
examples: Many a student has asked that same question.
He had made that drive many a time.
Many an evening ended with the two of them arguing about the thermostat.
Many a good idea has died in a committee meeting.
Many a parent learns that lesson the hard way.
Many's the night I fell asleep at that desk.
entries.pronunciation note: the a keeps its weak /ə/ and never takes stress here
entries.русский: не один, многие — книжн./устар.: большое число, но существительное в ед. числе
entries.position: predeterminer — the article a is locked inside the phrase, so no other determiner can appear: ✗ many a the student
entries.register: formal, literary, or deliberately old-fashioned; alive in proverbs, sermons, and sports commentary
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only — many a time, many a young writer, many a night. Never a plural noun (✗ many a times) and never an uncountable noun (✗ many a money). This is the one corner of English where many takes a singular, and the singular runs through the whole clause: Many a student has asked that question, never ✗ have asked.
entries.with of: never takes an of-phrase — ✗ many a of the students. Before a vowel sound the article changes as usual: many an evening. The only of-adjacent form is the archaic pronoun many a one.
entries.pattern: many a [singular countable] + singular verb · many an [vowel-initial singular noun] · many's the [singular noun] (fixed idiom)
entries.contrast: Many a student was late and many students were late mean the same thing with opposite grammar: many takes a plural noun and a plural verb, many a takes a singular of each. Do not confuse it with a good many and a great many, which are ordinary intensified many and take the plural — a good many students were late. The singular agreement is obligatory, not a stylistic option: ✗ many a parent have asked is an error. Modern American prose almost always prefers plain many; reach for many a only when the sentence wants that older cadence.
entries.variants: many an, many's the, many a one (archaic pronoun)
entries.see also: many, a great many, a good many, every, each, many's the, full many a

entries.meaning: Names a larger number or amount than something else — than a stated comparison, than before, or than what is already on hand. As a pronoun it stands alone with no noun after it: We need more, Would you like some more?
examples: We need more volunteers for Saturday.
Is there any more coffee in the pot?
She has more patience than I do.
Give me two more days and I'll have the draft.
More of the money went to overhead than to programs.
No more excuses — the report is due Friday.
There's soup on the stove if anyone wants more.
entries.русский: больше, ещё — сравнительная степень much и many
entries.position: central when it opens the noun phrase (more time); postdeterminer after a determiner or a numeral (some more coffee, no more excuses, two more days, many more people)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (more chairs, more people) and uncountable nouns (more time, more money). This is what makes it easy: more is the comparative of both many and much, so it is one of the few quantifiers here that never asks you to decide countability. It does not take a bare singular countable noun (✗ more chair).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — more of the cake, more of my time, more of them. Never ✗ more the cake. No of before a bare noun: more cake.
entries.pattern: more [plural/uncountable] · more [noun] than [phrase/clause] · more of [the/my/this + noun] · more of [them/it] · [some / no / any / two / many / much / a lot] more [noun] · the more … the more …
entries.contrast: More is the comparative of both many and much, and its two opposites split along the countability line: fewer for things you count, less for things you measure. Determiner against pronoun: more volunteers has a noun after it, we need more does not. Keep the determiner apart from the degree adverb — more chairs puts more in front of a noun, while more careful and more slowly put it in front of an adjective or adverb, where it is not a determiner at all. Watch the negatives too: no more means "none from here on" (No more excuses), not … anymore is about time (I don't work there anymore), and before a noun the two-word spelling is the right one (any more questions).
entries.variants: some more, no more, any more, a little more, a lot more, many more, much more, two more, the more … the more
entries.see also: most, many, much, fewer, less, how many more

entries.meaning: Names the majority — more than half, and usually a good deal more than half. Bare most generalizes about a whole class; most of picks the larger part out of a specific set. As a pronoun it stands alone: Most had already gone home.
examples: Most people would rather not fly on a Sunday night.
Most of the money is already spent.
She spends most of her time on the road.
Most information on that site is out of date.
Which team scored the most points?
Most of them had never seen snow before.
entries.русский: большинство, большая часть — больше половины
entries.position: central when it opens the noun phrase (most people); after the it forms the superlative of quantity (the most points)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (most people, most cities) and uncountable nouns (most information, most traffic). It does not take a bare singular countable noun (✗ most city), though most of the city is fine, because of reattaches it to an already-determined phrase.
entries.with of: required before another determiner or a pronoun — most of the students, most of my time, most of them. ✗ most the students is not standard written English. No of before a bare noun: most people.
entries.pattern: most [plural/uncountable] · most of [the/my/these + noun] · most of [them/it] · the most [noun] (superlative) · a most [adjective + singular noun] (formal intensifier)
entries.contrast: The bare/of split is a meaning split, not a style choice. Most people is generic — people at large. Most of the people is specific — the majority of one identified group. Against more, most is the superlative to its comparative, and both cover countables and uncountables alike, unlike their small-quantity opposites fewest and least, which do not. Three lookalikes to keep separate: the degree adverb (the most interesting talk), the formal intensifier meaning "very" (a most unusual request), and the colloquial regional most meaning "almost" (most everybody, most all of them), which is at home in American conversation and out of place in writing.
entries.variants: most of, the most, a most (intensifier), most all / most everybody (informal, "almost")
entries.see also: more, many, much, a majority of, the majority of, the minority of, least, all

entries.meaning: Marks a large but unspecified amount of something that cannot be counted. As a pronoun it stands alone: There isn't much to say.
examples: We don't have much time.
How much money did the repair cost?
There isn't much to say about it.
She spends too much energy worrying about things she can't control.
Much of the report was out of date before it was printed.
I didn't get much sleep last night.
entries.русский: много — только с неисчисляемыми; в утверждении звучит книжно, в речи a lot of
entries.position: central — it opens the noun phrase (much time); the identical degree adverb is a different animal (much better, thanks very much)
entries.register: neutral in questions and negatives; in a plain affirmative statement it is formal enough to sound stilted in American speech
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — much time, much money, much information. Never a plural countable noun (✗ much books, ✗ much people — use many) and never a singular countable noun (✗ much book).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — much of the report, much of my time, much of it. Never ✗ much the report. Bare much takes no of before a bare noun: much time.
entries.pattern: much [uncountable noun] · much of [the/my/this + noun] · much of [it/that] · how much [uncountable] · too / so / as / very / that much [uncountable] · much more [uncountable]
entries.contrast: Much is to uncountables what many is to plural countables. In affirmative statements Americans avoid bare much — We have much time is grammatical but nobody says it — and reach for a lot of or plenty of instead. Much survives in full health in questions (How much time do we have?), in negatives (not much time), and after too, so, as, how, very, and that. It is also entirely natural in affirmative writing the moment it is followed by of or fronted as a subject: Much of the report was wrong, Much remains to be done.
entries.variants: too much, so much, as much, how much, very much, that much, much of, much more, not much
entries.see also: many, more, a lot of, a great deal of, quite a bit of, little, not much, how much

entries.meaning: Names a large, uncounted quantity in casual speech — the conversational equivalent of a lot of, with no claim about how large.
examples: A bunch of us are going to the game on Saturday.
He left a bunch of dishes in the sink again.
That's going to cost a bunch of money we don't have.
A bunch of the emails never went out.
I've got a whole bunch of questions about the lease.
She picked up a bunch of bananas on the way home.
entries.pronunciation note: casually /ə ˈbʌntʃə/, "a buncha"
entries.русский: куча, полно — разг.: много чего угодно, без оценки размера
entries.position: central — the whole phrase fills the determiner slot
entries.register: informal American; everywhere in speech, out of place in formal writing
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (a bunch of people, a bunch of emails) and, in casual American speech, uncountable nouns as well (a bunch of money, a bunch of work, a bunch of time). The literal use is a different thing: a bunch of grapes, a bunch of keys, a bunch of flowers name a physical cluster, and there bunch is an ordinary head noun — the giveaway is that it pluralizes and takes its own modifiers (three big bunches of grapes), which the quantifier never does.
entries.with of: of is obligatory and welded to the phrase — ✗ a bunch people. Nothing changes before another determiner or a pronoun: a bunch of the emails, a bunch of them.
entries.pattern: a bunch of [plural countable] · a bunch of [uncountable] · a bunch of [the/my/these + noun] · a bunch of [them/us] · a whole bunch of [noun]
entries.contrast: A bunch of is the informal American twin of a lot of, and in speech the two swap freely. Agreement follows the noun after of, not bunch: A bunch of people are waiting (plural) beside A bunch of money is missing (singular). A prescriptive grammar would want is in the first, since bunch is singular, but notional plural agreement is what Americans actually say and write in informal registers. Against a couple of and a handful of, which name small numbers, a bunch of names a big one.
entries.variants: a whole bunch of, bunches of, a bunch (pronoun: thanks a bunch)
entries.see also: a lot of, lots of, tons of, a slew of, a couple of, a handful of

entries.meaning: Names a large quantity of anything, countable or not, without measuring it. It is the workhorse of spoken American quantity and the safe answer whenever much and many feel risky.
examples: A lot of people showed up for a Tuesday.
That job takes a lot of patience.
A lot of the paperwork was already done when we got there.
We wasted a lot of time on the wrong approach.
A lot of them had never voted in a primary before.
There's an awful lot of traffic on the bridge tonight.
entries.pronunciation note: in ordinary speech the t flaps and of reduces to /ə/: /ə ˈlɑɾə/, "a lotta"
entries.русский: много — нейтральный универсал: и с исчисляемыми, и с неисчисляемыми
entries.register: neutral to informal — the default in American speech and in most everyday writing; formal prose prefers much, many, a great deal of, or a large number of
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (a lot of people) and uncountable nouns (a lot of money). That coverage is the whole reason it took over the spoken language: it spares the speaker the much/many decision. Not used with a bare singular countable noun (✗ a lot of chair).
entries.with of: of is obligatory before a noun and cannot be dropped — ✗ a lot people. It stays put before another determiner or a pronoun: a lot of the money, a lot of them. Bare a lot with no of is either a pronoun (I have a lot) or an adverb (It helped a lot, a lot better).
entries.pattern: a lot of [plural/uncountable] · a lot of [the/my/these + noun] · a lot of [them/it] · quite a lot of [noun] · a whole lot of [noun] · an awful lot of [noun]
entries.contrast: A lot of is what Americans say where writing uses much and many. Verb agreement is decided by the noun after of and never by lot: A lot of people are waiting but A lot of time was wasted. Two spelling traps come with it — it is always two words (✗ alot), and the plural variant lots of is a genuine alternative, not an error. Against plenty of, a lot of only says the quantity is big; plenty of adds the promise that it is enough.
entries.variants: lots of, a whole lot of, quite a lot of, an awful lot of, a lotta (casual spelling)
entries.see also: lots of, quite a lot of, plenty of, a bunch of, much, many

entries.meaning: A casual, warm-toned a lot of. It reports a big quantity and makes no attempt to be precise about it.
examples: There were lots of kids at the pool this afternoon.
We still have lots of time before the movie starts.
She's got lots of ideas about how to fix the schedule.
Lots of the seats were still empty at kickoff.
He put lots of hot sauce on everything.
Lots of them come back a second year.
entries.pronunciation note: casually /ˈlɑtsə/
entries.русский: много, полно — разг., чуть проще и теплее, чем a lot of
entries.register: informal and conversational — a step more casual than a lot of, and the form adults use talking to children
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (lots of friends) and uncountable nouns (lots of sugar). Never a bare singular countable noun (✗ lots of chair).
entries.with of: of is obligatory before a noun — ✗ lots people. It stays before another determiner or a pronoun: lots of the candy, lots of them. Bare lots is a pronoun (We have lots).
entries.pattern: lots of [plural/uncountable] · lots of [the/my + noun] · lots of [them/it] · lots and lots of [noun]
entries.contrast: Lots of and a lot of mean exactly the same thing and differ only in register. The plural -s does not force a plural verb: agreement still follows the noun after of, so Lots of people are here but Lots of sugar is bad for you. Both are too casual for a research paper, where the equivalents are many, much, a great deal of, and a large number of.
entries.variants: lots and lots of, a lot of, loads of
entries.see also: a lot of, a bunch of, tons of, loads of, plenty of

entries.meaning: Marks a quantity that is large and, more to the point, sufficient — as much as anyone needs and then some.
examples: There's plenty of time before the train leaves.
We have plenty of parking behind the building.
He gave me plenty of reasons to be skeptical.
Plenty of people would take that job tomorrow.
There's plenty of room in the back seat for all three of you.
Don't worry about the food — there's plenty left.
entries.pronunciation note: the nt commonly reduces in American speech: /ˈplɛni ə/, "plenny a"
entries.русский: полно, вдоволь — много и притом достаточно, с запасом
entries.register: neutral to informal; usable almost anywhere short of a legal brief
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (plenty of chairs, plenty of reasons) and uncountable nouns (plenty of room, plenty of time). Never a bare singular countable noun (✗ plenty of chair).
entries.with of: of is obligatory before a noun — ✗ plenty chairs. Bare plenty is a pronoun (We have plenty) or, in casual American speech, an adverb meaning "quite" (plenty big, plenty warm enough).
entries.pattern: plenty of [plural/uncountable] · plenty of [the/my + noun] · plenty of [them/it] · plenty more [noun] · plenty [adjective] (informal adverb)
entries.contrast: Plenty of is not a synonym for a lot of. It adds sufficiency: the quantity is large and it is enough for the purpose, which is why it is the natural answer to worry — Don't rush, there's plenty of time. A lot of makes no such promise, and too much overshoots. Against enough, which marks the line exactly, plenty of sits comfortably above it. Agreement follows the noun after of: Plenty of seats are left, Plenty of time remains.
entries.variants: plenty more, plenty (pronoun), plenty (informal adverb), in plenty
entries.see also: enough, ample, a lot of, sufficient, aplenty, galore

entries.meaning: Names a quantity the speaker considers notably large — a mild intensification of a lot of, often with a raised eyebrow attached.
examples: That's quite a lot of money for a used dishwasher.
Quite a lot of people asked the same question afterward.
We got quite a lot of snow overnight.
He's put quite a lot of work into that yard.
Quite a lot of the data turned out to be duplicated.
She travels quite a lot for work.
entries.русский: довольно много — заметно большое количество, с лёгким удивлением
entries.register: neutral to informal; a shade more measured and more British-sounding than plain a lot of
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (quite a lot of people) and uncountable nouns (quite a lot of money). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory before a noun — ✗ quite a lot people. Bare quite a lot is a pronoun (She's read quite a lot) or an adverb (It helped quite a lot).
entries.pattern: quite a lot of [plural/uncountable] · quite a lot of [the/my + noun] · quite a lot of [them/it] · quite a lot (pronoun or adverb)
entries.contrast: Quite in front of a lot of, a few, and a bit of is an intensifier, not a hedge: quite a lot of trouble is more trouble than a lot of trouble, not less. The same quite in front of a bare adjective can go the other way in American English (quite good often means only "fairly good"), and that split is what confuses learners. Treat quite a lot of, quite a few, and quite a bit of as three fixed phrases that all mean "a large amount or number."
entries.variants: quite a bit of, quite a few, quite a number of, quite a lot (pronoun)
entries.see also: a lot of, quite a few, quite a bit of, a fair amount of, a bit of

entries.meaning: Names a large, accumulated, coherent mass of evidence, work, or knowledge — quantity presented as one organized whole rather than as a heap.
examples: A growing body of evidence links the two conditions.
Her body of work spans four decades and three countries.
There is a substantial body of research on the question and no consensus anywhere in it.
The ruling unsettles a body of case law going back to the 1970s.
A body of knowledge that takes a decade to acquire cannot be replaced in a summer.
Lake Michigan is the largest body of water inside a single state.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is the weak /ə/ and of reduces to /ə/ in ordinary speech: /ə ˈbɑdi ə/
entries.русский: свод, корпус — большой связный массив данных, знаний, работ
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in academic, legal, and journalistic prose
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns that name something accumulated — a body of evidence, a body of work, a body of research, a body of law, a body of knowledge, a body of literature. It reaches a plural only when the plural is itself being treated as one collection (a body of laws, a body of texts); ordinary countable plurals are out (✗ a body of chairs, ✗ a body of emails), and so are physical substances (✗ a body of sugar). The literal senses are a different word: a body of water is a geographic term and a body of troops an older military one, and in both body is a real head noun that pluralizes freely — two bodies of water.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a body evidence. It stays before another determiner: a body of the case law that predates the statute.
entries.pattern: a body of [mass abstract] · a body of [the + mass abstract] · a growing / substantial / considerable / large body of [noun] · the body of [noun] (definite, naming the whole)
entries.contrast: A body of is not a plain a lot of: it claims the quantity is large and coherent — one accumulated mass that hangs together and can be argued about. That is why a growing body of evidence is the standard phrase and ✗ a body of noise is not. Against a wealth of, which approves of what it counts, and a great deal of, which measures and nothing more, a body of organizes. The verb is singular, since body is the head and the noun after of is a mass: A body of research suggests otherwise.
entries.variants: a growing body of, a substantial body of, a large body of, the body of, bodies of
entries.see also: a wealth of, a great deal of, a large amount of, considerable, a multitude of

entries.meaning: The bare ancestor of a good deal of — a large amount of something uncountable. In American English today it is a period form, not an option.
examples: It gave the old man a deal of trouble before he was done with it.
There was a deal of talk in the village that winter and very little sense in it.
He had spent a deal of money on the place and had nothing to show for it.
"I've heard a deal of nonsense in my time," the judge said, "but never so much in one afternoon."
Those letters cost her a deal of pains to write and were never answered.
A modern editor would change every one of them to a good deal of.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is the weak /ə/, never /eɪ/, and of reduces to /əv/ or a bare /ə/
entries.русский: изрядно, немало — устар./диал., голый предок a good deal of
entries.register: archaic and dialectal. The bare form dropped out of standard American English in the nineteenth century and survives now only in period prose, in reported country speech, and in British and Irish dialect. With an adjective wedged in, the same phrase is perfectly current: a good deal of, a great deal of
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — a deal of trouble, a deal of money, a deal of talk. Never a plural countable noun: ✗ a deal of people, ✗ a deal of reasons. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a deal trouble. It stays before another determiner: a deal of the money was gone.
entries.pattern: a deal of [uncountable] · a deal of [the/his + uncountable] · a deal [comparative] (dated adverb: a deal better) · compare current a good deal of / a great deal of
entries.contrast: This is the ancestor of a good deal of and a great deal of, and the only difference between them is the adjective the modern phrases keep. Do not write bare a deal of in present-day American English: it reads as costume rather than register. When you meet it in Dickens, in Twain, or in an 1880 deposition, read it as plain much. Keep it clear of the thoroughly current noun a deal meaning a bargain or an arrangement (We made a deal, a good deal on the car), which is unrelated to quantity.
entries.variants: a good deal of, a great deal of, a deal more, a deal (dated adverb)
entries.see also: a good deal of, a great deal of, much, a power of, a sight of

entries.meaning: Names a quantity that is respectably large without being remarkable — more than a little, less than a flood.
examples: It takes a fair amount of practice before it feels natural.
We got a fair amount of rain over the weekend.
There's still a fair amount of work left on the second floor.
She's put a fair amount of her own money into the business.
A fair amount of the equipment was already obsolete.
I've spent a fair amount of time thinking about this.
entries.русский: довольно много, порядочно — немало, но без изумления
entries.register: neutral; common in speech and in unfussy writing
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — a fair amount of money, a fair amount of work, a fair amount of rain. For countable things the parallel phrase is a fair number of — a fair number of people, never ✗ a fair amount of people in careful writing.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a fair amount money. It stays before another determiner: a fair amount of the budget, a fair amount of it.
entries.pattern: a fair amount of [uncountable] · a fair amount of [the/my + uncountable] · a fair amount of [it] · compare a fair number of [plural countable]
entries.contrast: The amount / number split is the same countability line that separates much from many, and this pair is where it is easiest to hear. A fair amount of is a deliberate hedge: it claims a moderate-to-large quantity without committing to "a lot." Within the family it is the smallest — a fair amount of < a good deal of < a great deal of. Note that fair here means "considerable," not "just" or "average."
entries.variants: a fair number of, a fair bit of, a fair amount
entries.see also: a good deal of, a large amount of, quite a lot of, a number of, a bit of

entries.meaning: Names a substantial amount of something uncountable, presented as worth noticing.
examples: The project has taken a good deal of time and money.
There's a good deal of truth in what she said.
He put a good deal of thought into that letter.
A good deal of the criticism was fair.
It cost me a good deal of sleep before I decided.
The new engine is a good deal quieter.
entries.русский: немало, изрядно — существенное количество неисчисляемого
entries.register: neutral, leaning slightly formal or writerly
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — a good deal of money, a good deal of trouble, a good deal of attention. Never a plural countable noun: ✗ a good deal of people, ✗ a good deal of problems. The countable partner is a good many, which takes a plural noun and no of.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a good deal money. It stays before another determiner or a pronoun: a good deal of the money, a good deal of it.
entries.pattern: a good deal of [uncountable] · a good deal of [the/my/this + uncountable] · a good deal of [it] · a good deal [comparative adjective] (adverb: a good deal better)
entries.contrast: A good deal of and a great deal of are the same construction with a different adjective; great is the stronger of the two. Both are uncountable-only, and that is the trap — their countable counterparts are a good many and a great many, which look nothing like them. Keep the quantifier apart from the ordinary noun phrase a good deal meaning a bargain (We got a good deal on the car) and from the adverb (a good deal better, a good deal more expensive).
entries.variants: a great deal of, a good deal (adverb), a good bit of
entries.see also: a great deal of, a good many, a fair amount of, much, a deal of

entries.meaning: Names a large amount of something uncountable. In edited American prose it is the most common formal alternative to a lot of.
examples: The study required a great deal of patience.
There is a great deal of evidence pointing the other way.
She has a great deal of experience with cases like this.
A great deal of the money never reached the schools.
It would save us a great deal of trouble later.
That one paragraph explains a great deal.
entries.русский: очень много, весьма значительное количество — книжн., с неисчисляемыми
entries.register: neutral to formal — the standard written phrase where speech would say a lot of
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — a great deal of money, a great deal of evidence, a great deal of effort. Never a plural countable noun: ✗ a great deal of people, ✗ a great deal of studies. The countable partner is a great many.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a great deal money. It stays before another determiner or a pronoun: a great deal of the evidence, a great deal of it.
entries.pattern: a great deal of [uncountable] · a great deal of [the/my/this + uncountable] · a great deal of [it] · a great deal (pronoun: That explains a great deal) · a great deal [comparative] (adverb)
entries.contrast: A great deal of is the formal register's a lot of for uncountables — the phrase that lets a paper avoid both the casual a lot of and the stilted bare much. Its countable twin is a great many, and the two are not interchangeable: ✗ a great deal of reasons and ✗ a great many evidence are both wrong. A good deal of says the same thing a notch quieter.
entries.variants: a good deal of, a great deal (pronoun), a great deal (adverb), a very great deal of
entries.see also: a good deal of, a great many, a large amount of, much, a wealth of

entries.meaning: Names a large measured quantity of something uncountable. The adjective is freely swapped for emphasis — huge, vast, enormous, tremendous — without changing the grammar.
examples: The process uses a large amount of water.
They collected a large amount of data over three winters.
A large amount of money went missing between the two accounts.
Storing large amounts of video is not cheap.
A large amount of the damage was invisible from the street.
That takes a huge amount of preparation.
entries.русский: большое количество — с неисчисляемыми; книжн. и деловой стиль
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in reports, science writing, and journalism
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — a large amount of money, a large amount of data, a large amount of water. Never a plural countable noun: ✗ a large amount of people, ✗ a large amount of errors. The countable phrase is a large number of. Two nouns cause trouble here because they feel plural but are grammatically uncountable in English — data and traffic — so a large amount of data is correct.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a large amount money. It stays before another determiner or a pronoun: a large amount of the funding, a large amount of it.
entries.pattern: a large amount of [uncountable] · large amounts of [uncountable] · a large amount of [the/this + uncountable] · a large amount of [it]
entries.contrast: This entry and a large number of are the two halves of the single most-corrected error in the quantifier system. Amount goes with what you measure, number with what you count: a large amount of sugar but a large number of sugar cubes. When you cannot decide, the escape hatch is a lot of, which takes either. The deal phrases (a great deal of, a good deal of) behave identically to amount but have no countable version at all.
entries.variants: a great amount of, a huge amount of, a vast amount of, an enormous amount of, large amounts of
entries.see also: a large number of, a great deal of, a fair amount of, much, a lot of

entries.meaning: Names a large and valuable supply of something — the size of the quantity and the speaker's approval of it come as one package.
examples: She brings a wealth of experience to the job.
The archive holds a wealth of material on the 1930s.
There's a wealth of detail in the footnotes.
The new park gives the neighborhood a wealth of options for a Saturday.
He had a wealth of stories about the old newsroom.
A wealth of the detail in that book comes from letters found in an attic.
entries.русский: богатство, изобилие — много и притом ценного, с одобрением
entries.register: neutral to formal; a favorite of book jackets and job applications
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (a wealth of experience, a wealth of detail, a wealth of information) and plural countable nouns (a wealth of options, a wealth of resources). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a wealth information. It stays before another determiner: a wealth of the material we collected.
entries.pattern: a wealth of [uncountable] · a wealth of [plural countable] · a wealth of [the/his + noun]
entries.contrast: A wealth of carries a built-in positive judgment: the quantity is large and that is a good thing. This is why a wealth of experience is natural and a wealth of problems is not — for a large quantity of something unwelcome, use a host of, a slew of, or no end of. Compare an abundance of, which is positive but neutral about value, and a plethora of, which historically meant an unwelcome excess. Agreement follows the noun after of.
entries.variants: a wealth of experience, an abundance of, a treasure trove of, a fund of
entries.see also: abundant, a great deal of, a host of, ample, plenty of

entries.meaning: Names a quantity past the right one — large, and larger than it should be.
examples: The refund was issued in an excess of caution rather than as any admission of fault.
An excess of rain in June cost the growers most of the crop.
He lost the account through an excess of enthusiasm and a shortage of preparation.
The study found an excess of respiratory cases in the three counties nearest the plant.
There is an excess of opinion on the subject and almost no data.
The winning bid came in in excess of four million dollars, which says how much and not too much.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is the weak /ən/; the noun keeps its stress on the second syllable, while the attributive adjective in excess baggage moves it to the first, /ˈɛksɛs/
entries.русский: избыток, излишек — больше, чем следует
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in medicine, finance, statistics, and careful prose
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns above all — an excess of caution, an excess of zeal, an excess of moisture, an excess of enthusiasm. It takes a plural countable noun when the count is being measured against an expected figure, which is the statistical use — an excess of deaths over the seasonal average, an excess of applications. Never a bare singular countable noun: ✗ an excess of chair.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ an excess caution. Do not confuse it with the approximator in excess of, which attaches to a number and means "more than" (in excess of $2 million); that one is homed with the numerals.
entries.pattern: an excess of [uncountable] · an excess of [plural countable] (statistical) · in an excess of [noun] (adverbial: in an excess of caution) · excess [noun] (attributive adjective: excess baggage) · compare in excess of [number]
entries.contrast: This is not a neutral large quantity. An excess of says the amount is past what is wanted, needed, or safe, which is why an excess of caution is a gentle apology and an excess of fluid is a diagnosis. A lot of and a great deal of pass no judgment at all; a plethora of and a surfeit of pass the same judgment this does. The near-twin in excess of is a different construction with a different meaning: an excess of applicants means too many, in excess of 200 applicants means more than 200.
entries.variants: in an excess of, a surfeit of, an overabundance of, excess (attributive adjective), excessive
entries.see also: a plethora of, a large amount of, enough, ample, upwards of, in excess of

entries.meaning: Names an unlimited or indefinitely large amount — "as much as it takes, and the speaker is not counting."
examples: He'll spend any amount of time on a problem that interests him.
They would have paid any amount of money to get that tape back.
There are any number of reasons the deal could still fall apart.
You can throw any amount of money at the bridge and the traffic won't improve.
No amount of explaining was going to change her mind.
She has any amount of patience with beginners.
entries.русский: сколько угодно — неограниченно много, говорящий не считает
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — any amount of money, any amount of time, any amount of trouble. The countable partner is any number of — any number of reasons — and in American English that one is far the more common of the two.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ any amount money. Before another determiner it holds: any amount of the profit.
entries.pattern: any amount of [uncountable] · any number of [plural countable] · no amount of [uncountable] (the negative counterpart)
entries.contrast: In an affirmative statement this is a large-quantity idiom, not ordinary free-choice any: He'll spend any amount of time on a problem he likes means a great deal of time, however much it takes. Under negation the phrase flips to its mirror image no amount of, which is emphatic and very common — No amount of practice was going to fix that swing. Keep it apart from plain any, which is the free-choice determiner, and remember that any number of is the version you need for countable nouns.
entries.variants: any number of, no amount of, any amount
entries.see also: any, a great deal of, a large number of, no end of, countless

entries.meaning: Names a large amount of something uncountable, with the speaker mildly registering the size — "more than you would think."
examples: That repair is going to take quite a bit of time.
We got quite a bit of rain out of Thursday's storm.
He has put quite a bit of work into the application.
Quite a bit of the money had already been spent by then.
There's quite a bit of interest in the second session.
She knows quite a bit about early jazz.
entries.pronunciation note: both little words are weak — a /ə/ and of /əv/, and in ordinary speech the t flaps and of reduces: /ˌkwaɪt ə ˈbɪɾə/, "quite a bidda"
entries.русский: порядочно, немало — разг., с неисчисляемыми: больше, чем кажется
entries.register: neutral to informal; very common in American speech and unremarkable in ordinary writing
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — quite a bit of money, quite a bit of time, quite a bit of work. Never a plural countable noun (✗ quite a bit of people, ✗ quite a bit of reasons — the countable phrase is quite a few) and never a bare singular countable noun (✗ quite a bit of chair).
entries.with of: of is obligatory and welded to the phrase — ✗ quite a bit money. It stays before another determiner or a pronoun: quite a bit of the money, quite a bit of it. Bare quite a bit with no of is either a pronoun (She knows quite a bit) or an adverb (It helped quite a bit, quite a bit better).
entries.pattern: quite a bit of [uncountable] · quite a bit of [the/my/this + uncountable] · quite a bit of [it] · quite a bit (pronoun or adverb) · compare quite a few [plural countable]
entries.contrast: It contains a bit and it means much. A bit of trouble is a small amount; quite a bit of trouble is a large one — the same inversion that turns a few into quite a few, and there is no way to derive either from the parts. The pair splits on countability exactly as much and many do: quite a bit of money against quite a few dollars, never ✗ quite a bit of dollars. Distribution is the other half of the lesson: this is an affirmative phrase and one of the standard American repairs for stilted bare much — We have quite a bit of time where writing would say We have much time — while much keeps the questions and the negatives, where quite a bit of is at best awkward: you ask How much time do we have?, not Do we have quite a bit of time? Agreement follows the noun after of, which for an uncountable is always singular: Quite a bit of the money is still unspent.
entries.variants: quite a bit, quite a little bit of, quite a few, quite a lot of
entries.see also: quite a few, quite a lot of, a good deal of, much, a bit of

entries.meaning: Names a sizable group of people or creatures arriving together, in a light journalistic register.
examples: The governor arrived with a bevy of aides and no answers.
A bevy of startups turned up promising the same thing.
A bevy of quail broke out of the brush ahead of the dogs.
The premiere drew a bevy of second-tier celebrities and one genuine star.
A bevy of new regulations takes effect in January.
She fielded a bevy of questions about the budget before anyone asked about the schools.
entries.русский: стайка, целая группа — журн., о группе людей или живых существ
entries.register: informal to journalistic and faintly jocular — a headline and society-page word. Applied to women (a bevy of beauties) it is dated and now reads as leering, which is worth knowing before anyone uses it that way
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns, and above all ones naming people or animals — a bevy of aides, a bevy of celebrities, a bevy of quail. Loose journalism extends it to things (a bevy of new features), which is standard enough but flattens the word. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ a bevy of information. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a bevy lawyers. It stays before another determiner: a bevy of the usual consultants.
entries.pattern: a bevy of [plural countable, usually animate] · a bevy of [the/these + plural] · a whole bevy of [plural]
entries.contrast: Bevy began as a hunting collective for quail and larks, and the flock is still audible in it: the phrase pictures the group arriving together and slightly fluttering. That tone is what separates it from the neutral a host of and the brisk a slew of, neither of which pictures anything. Agreement is notional and normally plural: A bevy of consultants were brought in.
entries.variants: a whole bevy of, a covey of, a flock of, a host of
entries.see also: a host of, a slew of, hordes of, droves of, a multitude of

entries.meaning: Names a sizable number of countable things, with a note of the speaker having taken stock — "more than you would guess."
examples: A good many people showed up in spite of the weather.
He's been doing this for a good many years.
A good many of the houses on that block have sold since spring.
There are a good many reasons not to sign that lease.
I've read a good many of them, but not all.
We'll need a good many more volunteers before Saturday.
entries.русский: немало, порядочно — с исчисляемыми; чуть старомодный, простецкий оттенок
entries.register: neutral, with a homespun or slightly old-fashioned flavor; common in Southern and Midwestern speech
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — a good many people, a good many years, a good many of the houses. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ a good many money, ✗ a good many information. The uncountable partner is a good deal of.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — a good many of the applicants, a good many of them. No of before a bare plural: a good many applicants, never ✗ a good many of applicants.
entries.pattern: a good many [plural countable] · a good many of [the/my/these + plural] · a good many of [them/us] · a good many more [plural]
entries.contrast: Look at the syntax before you object to it: the singular article a stands in front of the plural quantifier many, and the phrase then takes a plural noun and a plural verb — A good many people were unhappy. It is fully standard. Its uncountable counterpart is a good deal of, and its stronger, more formal sibling is a great many. Against plain many, a good many is warmer and more conversational.
entries.variants: a great many, a good many more, a good few
entries.see also: a great many, many, a good deal of, quite a few, a few

entries.meaning: Names an emphatically large number of countable things — many, with the volume turned up.
examples: A great many people were affected by the recall.
She has written a great many essays on the subject.
A great many of the original documents were lost in the fire.
There are a great many things I would do differently.
A great many of them never finished the program.
It has been repeated by a great many otherwise careful writers.
entries.русский: весьма многие, великое множество — усиленное many
entries.register: neutral to formal; at home in written English and in careful speech
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — a great many people, a great many books. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ a great many evidence, ✗ a great many money. The uncountable partner is a great deal of.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — a great many of the delegates, a great many of them. No of before a bare plural: a great many delegates.
entries.pattern: a great many [plural countable] · a great many of [the/these + plural] · a great many of [them] · a great many more [plural]
entries.contrast: A great many and a great deal of are a matched pair split by countability, and swapping them is a hard error: ✗ a great deal of reasons, ✗ a great many evidence. Against a good many, a great many is stronger and more formal. Against plain many, it is emphatic — it is the phrase a writer uses when many alone would undersell the number. Note again the singular a in front of a plural quantifier, and note that the verb still agrees plural.
entries.variants: a good many, a great many more, a very great many
entries.see also: a good many, a great deal of, many, numerous, a large number of

entries.meaning: Names a large and varied number of countable things arriving together, most often problems or considerations.
examples: The merger raises a host of regulatory questions.
She turned down the job for a host of reasons.
A host of small errors added up to a serious problem.
The bill would create a whole host of new exemptions.
A host of startups have tried the same idea and failed.
There are a host of reasons to be careful with that number.
entries.русский: масса, целый ряд — много и разного, чаще всего проблем
entries.register: neutral to formal; a staple of journalism and business writing
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a host of problems, a host of reasons, a host of new rules. It does not take uncountable nouns in careful writing (✗ a host of information), and never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a host problems. It stays before another determiner: a host of the issues we raised.
entries.pattern: a host of [plural countable] · a host of [the/these + plural] · a whole host of [plural countable]
entries.contrast: A host of is neutral in form but skews toward the unwelcome in practice: its favorite companions are problems, issues, questions, complications, and challenges, where a wealth of takes the good things. Agreement is notional and normally plural — A host of new rules are taking effect Monday. Keep it separate from the ordinary noun host (the person giving the party, the host of a show) and from a host of in its older military sense, an army.
entries.variants: a whole host of, a raft of, a battery of, an array of
entries.see also: a slew of, a multitude of, numerous, a wealth of, a large number of

entries.meaning: Names a large count of individual things, stated with enough formality to survive in a report or a paper.
examples: A large number of students were absent that week.
The survey drew a large number of responses from rural counties.
Large numbers of birds pass through the refuge in October.
A large number of the files had never been opened.
The change affects a large number of small businesses.
A large number of them declined to give their names.
entries.русский: большое число — с исчисляемыми; книжн., научный и деловой стиль
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard phrase in academic, technical, and business writing
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — a large number of students, a large number of errors, a large number of the applicants. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ a large number of money, ✗ a large number of information. The uncountable phrase is a large amount of.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a large number students. It stays before another determiner or a pronoun: a large number of the applicants, a large number of them.
entries.pattern: a large number of [plural countable] + plural verb · large numbers of [plural countable] · a large number of [the/these + plural] · a large number of [them]
entries.contrast: Two rules meet in this phrase. First, the countability rule: number counts, amount measures, so a large number of bottles but a large amount of water. Second, the agreement rule that catches native writers as often as learners: a number of takes a plural verb (A large number of students were absent), while the number of takes a singular one (The number of students was surprising). The indefinite article turns the phrase into a quantifier; the definite article leaves number as the real head noun.
entries.variants: a great number of, a huge number of, a vast number of, large numbers of, a number of
entries.see also: a large amount of, a number of, many, numerous, a majority of

entries.meaning: Names more than half of a set — the counted larger part, as opposed to the impressionistic "a lot."
examples: A majority of voters said they had already made up their minds.
A majority of the states have passed some version of the law.
The measure needs a majority of the votes cast, not of the members present.
A majority of them had been with the company under five years.
A vast majority of the complaints came from one zip code.
A majority of the committee was in favor of postponing.
entries.русский: большинство — подсчитанная бо́льшая часть, более половины
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in reporting, polling, and law
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a majority of voters, a majority of the states, a majority of them. It also takes a singular mass that names a share rather than a count (a majority of the vote, a majority of the budget), and there the verb goes singular. It never takes an ordinary uncountable substance: ✗ a majority of water.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a majority voters. The noun after of is normally definite or generic: a majority of the committee, a majority of Americans.
entries.pattern: a majority of [plural countable] + plural verb · a majority of [the + collective/mass] + singular verb · a vast / slim / overwhelming majority of [plural]
entries.contrast: A majority of against the majority of: the definite version is the everyday one and points at an identified group, while the indefinite is a shade more statistical and is what you want after a vote count. Agreement is notional either way — plural when the phrase counts people or things (A majority of voters were undecided), singular when it names one body or one share (A majority of the committee was in favor). Against most, which says the same thing in one word and needs no of before a bare noun — most voters beside a majority of voters. A majority is anything past half; for a lopsided one you need the vast majority.
entries.variants: the majority of, a vast majority of, an overwhelming majority of, a slim majority of, a bare majority of
entries.see also: most, the majority of, the minority of, the bulk of, percent, a plurality of, a supermajority of

entries.meaning: Names a large number of things of many different kinds — number and diversity together, in a formal register.
examples: The failure had a multiplicity of causes, and the report names none of them.
Equity will intervene to avoid a multiplicity of suits arising from one transaction.
A multiplicity of standards has kept the industry from settling on a single connector.
The program is administered through a multiplicity of state agencies with overlapping jurisdiction.
She traced a multiplicity of small errors back to one bad assumption.
In plainer prose a multiplicity of factors is simply many different factors.
entries.pronunciation note: the t of -city flaps to /ɾ/ in American speech, exactly as in majority and variety
entries.русский: множественность, многообразие — книжн.: много и притом разного рода
entries.register: formal and technical — academic prose, engineering, and legal drafting. In ordinary writing it is heavy and faintly bureaucratic, and an editor will usually cut it to many or a variety of
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a multiplicity of factors, a multiplicity of causes, a multiplicity of forms. Uncountable nouns read as an error in careful prose: ✗ a multiplicity of information. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a multiplicity factors. It stays before another determiner: a multiplicity of the same objections.
entries.pattern: a multiplicity of [plural countable] · a multiplicity of [the/these + plural] · a multiplicity of suits (the legal set phrase)
entries.contrast: A multiplicity of stresses kinds, not headcount: it says the things are many and of many different sorts, which is why a multiplicity of causes is idiomatic and a multiplicity of people is not. Against a multitude of, which is about sheer number, and a variety of, which says the same thing in a register anyone can read. American legal writing gives it a near-technical sense — a multiplicity of suits names the problem that joinder rules exist to prevent, several lawsuits where one would do.
entries.variants: a multitude of, a variety of, manifold, multiplicities of (rare)
entries.see also: a multitude of, a variety of, myriad, numerous, manifold

entries.meaning: Names a very large number of countable things, viewed as a crowd rather than a list.
examples: The delay had a multitude of causes, none of them decisive.
A good coat of paint covers a multitude of sins.
A multitude of small charges had piled up on the account.
Multitudes of travelers were stranded when the system went down.
The decision affects a multitude of people who had no say in it.
He offered a multitude of excuses, each less convincing than the last.
entries.русский: множество, тьма — книжн.: очень много, воспринятое как толпа
entries.register: formal or literary; slightly grand for everyday speech
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a multitude of reasons, a multitude of small decisions. Uncountable nouns appear with it only in elevated or biblical style; the plural is the norm. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a multitude reasons. It stays before another determiner: a multitude of the smaller towns.
entries.pattern: a multitude of [plural countable] · a multitude of [the/these + plural] · multitudes of [plural countable] · cover a multitude of sins (fixed idiom)
entries.contrast: A multitude of is the elevated register's a lot of, and it shares its ground with a host of and a myriad of. Where a host of leans toward trouble and a wealth of toward good fortune, a multitude is neutral about value and emphatic about sheer number. Agreement is notional and usually plural (A multitude of factors are involved). The idiom cover a multitude of sins — a phrase from the King James Bible now used lightly of anything that hides a lot of flaws — is fixed and cannot be varied.
entries.variants: multitudes of, a myriad of, a host of, cover a multitude of sins
entries.see also: a host of, myriad, countless, numerous, a multiplicity of

entries.meaning: Names a large number of things, in careful use an unhelpfully large number — an oversupply rather than merely a lot.
examples: The menu offers a plethora of options and no way to choose among them.
A plethora of new apps promise to do the same thing.
There is a plethora of research on the topic and very little agreement.
The form asks for a plethora of details nobody will ever read.
A plethora of competing standards slowed the rollout.
He answered with a plethora of statistics and no actual argument.
entries.pronunciation note: stress falls on the first syllable; the common /pləˈθɔrə/ is a mispronunciation
entries.русский: переизбыток — книжн.: не просто много, а больше, чем нужно
entries.register: formal, often self-consciously so; heavily overused in business and marketing prose
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a plethora of options, a plethora of choices. Uncountable nouns occur (a plethora of information) but are less established. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a plethora options. Bare plethora without an article is nonstandard in American English: ✗ plethora of options.
entries.pattern: a plethora of [plural countable] · a plethora of [the/these + plural] · a veritable plethora of [plural]
entries.contrast: Plethora came into English as a medical term for a dangerous excess — too much of something — and careful writers still use it that way, so a plethora of options implies more options than are useful. In current American usage it has drifted to a plain "a lot of," which is why editors often strike it: if you mean many, many is shorter and clearer. If you do want the note of excess, a surfeit of and an overabundance of keep it intact.
entries.variants: a surfeit of, an overabundance of, a superfluity of, a veritable plethora of
entries.see also: a multitude of, a host of, myriad, numerous, countless

entries.meaning: Names a set of things spread out along some scale — several to many, differing from one another by degree.
examples: The clinic offers a range of services on a sliding scale.
We tested the alloy across a wide range of temperatures.
A range of options was presented and none of them was cheap.
The bill drew objections from a range of groups that agree on nothing else.
She has worked on a broad range of cases, from zoning disputes to capital appeals.
The store stocks shoes in a range of widths, which is rarer than it sounds.
entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /ə/ in ordinary speech: /ə ˈreɪndʒə/
entries.русский: ряд, диапазон — набор вещей, различающихся по степени
entries.register: neutral to formal; a workhorse of business, policy, medical, and academic prose
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a range of options, a range of services, a range of temperatures. It takes an uncountable noun only where that noun names something measurable along a scale (a range of motion, a range of experience); ✗ a range of information is odd. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a range options. It stays before another determiner: a range of the products we already carry.
entries.pattern: a range of [plural countable] · a wide / broad / full / whole range of [plural] · a range of [the/these + plural] · the range of [noun] (definite, naming the span itself)
entries.contrast: A range of claims spread along a scale: the things differ from one end to the other in price, size, difficulty, or temperature. A variety of claims assortment with no ordering at all — a range of prices runs from low to high, a variety of flavors runs from nowhere to nowhere. Both are far weaker quantity words than they look: a range of options can be four options, which is exactly why press releases like the phrase. Agreement is notional and usually plural (A range of products are affected), though a writer treating range as the head noun will use the singular.
entries.variants: a wide range of, a broad range of, a full range of, a whole range of, ranges of
entries.see also: a variety of, a multiplicity of, a series of, a host of, all kinds of, all sorts of

entries.meaning: Names a number of things arriving one after another — quantity with sequence attached.
examples: A series of small mistakes ended with the wrong address on four thousand envelopes.
The city held a series of public meetings that changed nothing.
A series of storms came through the valley in the same week.
He answered with a string of excuses, each thinner than the last.
The paper documents a series of failures in the inspection process.
After a string of one-run losses the team fired the hitting coach.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun is spelled and pronounced the same in the singular and the plural — one series, two series; there is no ✗ a serie
entries.русский: серия, ряд — несколько подряд, одно за другим
entries.register: neutral; at home everywhere from news copy to a lab report
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns naming events, steps, or items that follow one another — a series of meetings, a series of errors, a series of storms. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ a series of information, ✗ a series of trouble. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a series meetings. It stays before another determiner: a series of the same complaints.
entries.pattern: a series of [plural countable] · a whole series of [plural] · a series of [the/these + plural] · a string / succession / run / chain of [plural]
entries.contrast: A series of adds succession to number: the things came one after another, in time or in order, which is the whole difference from a bunch of, which says nothing about sequence. Its informal twin a string of says the same thing with a shrug and a hint that the run was unbroken and unwelcome — a string of burglaries, a string of bad dates — while a run of stresses the streak and a succession of is the formal choice. In careful writing the verb is singular, because series is the head noun: A series of meetings was scheduled. Notional plural agreement (were scheduled) is common in speech and increasingly in print.
entries.variants: a string of, a succession of, a run of, a chain of, a whole series of
entries.see also: a range of, a wave of, a slew of, a host of, dozens of

entries.meaning: Names a large number of countable things appearing at once, in a briskly informal American register.
examples: The announcement drew a slew of angry emails.
A slew of new restaurants opened on that block last year.
She has a slew of reasons for wanting out of the contract.
The report contains a slew of recommendations nobody intends to follow.
A slew of the early applicants withdrew before the interview.
They released a whole slew of updates in a single week.
entries.русский: куча, целый ворох — разг. амер.: много сразу
entries.register: informal to journalistic American; common in news writing, rare outside North America
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a slew of complaints, a slew of new hires. Not used with uncountable nouns (✗ a slew of money) and never with a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a slew complaints. It stays before another determiner: a slew of the smaller banks.
entries.pattern: a slew of [plural countable] · a slew of [the/these + plural] · a whole slew of [plural]
entries.contrast: American near-synonyms sort by nuance: a slew of is neutral about good and bad and simply says "a lot of, arriving together"; a spate of insists the events came in a sudden burst (a spate of burglaries); a raft of is more common in policy writing; a bunch of is the most casual of the four. Slew here has nothing to do with the verb slay — it comes from Irish sluagh, a crowd.
entries.variants: a whole slew of, a spate of, a raft of, a rash of
entries.see also: a bunch of, a host of, dozens of, a wave of, numerous

entries.meaning: Names a number of things of different kinds — diversity first, quantity second.
examples: The store carries a wide variety of flours, none of them cheap.
She left the job for a variety of reasons and named exactly one of them.
A variety of approaches have been tried and none has been evaluated.
The grant supports a variety of after-school programs across the district.
Those symptoms can be caused by a variety of things, most of them harmless.
Honeycrisp is a variety of apple, which is one apple and not a crowd.
entries.pronunciation note: the first syllable of variety is the weak /və/, never /væ/, and the t flaps to /ɾ/
entries.русский: разные, целый ряд — сначала разнообразие, потом количество
entries.register: neutral; standard in every register short of poetry, and one of the commonest hedges in American writing
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a variety of reasons, a variety of products, a variety of ways. Uncountables only when the noun names a kind rather than a substance: a variety of music is fine, ✗ a variety of water is not. It does take a singular countable noun in the unrelated botanical sense, where a variety of apple names one cultivar and means the opposite of a large quantity.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a variety reasons. It stays before another determiner: a variety of the same excuses.
entries.pattern: a variety of [plural countable] · a wide / great / rich / whole variety of [plural] · a variety of [the + plural] · for a variety of reasons (fixed) · compare a variety of [singular] = one cultivar
entries.contrast: The claim is assortment, not size: a variety of reasons is several reasons of different kinds and can be three of them. That makes it the polite way to be vague, and for a variety of reasons is the standard American refusal to give any. Against a range of, which spreads its items along a scale; against a multiplicity of, which says the same thing in a lab coat; against a host of and a slew of, which claim a big number and no diversity at all. Agreement is notional and usually plural: A variety of factors are at work. And watch the singular trap — a variety of apple is one apple, not many.
entries.variants: a wide variety of, a great variety of, a rich variety of, a whole variety of, varieties of
entries.see also: a range of, a multiplicity of, myriad, a host of, all kinds of, all sorts of

entries.meaning: Names a large number of things arriving together in a surge that rises and passes — and, with an abstract noun, a feeling that comes over someone the same way.
examples: A wave of layoffs hit the industry in the second quarter.
She felt a wave of relief when the phone finally rang.
The bill set off a flurry of amendments in the last week of the session.
A wave of new arrivals doubled the town's population in a decade.
Waves of thunderstorms moved across the state all afternoon.
There was a flurry of activity at the front desk and then nothing for an hour.
entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /ə/ in speech: /ə ˈweɪvə/
entries.русский: волна — наплыв чего-либо; с абстрактным сущ. — нахлынувшее чувство
entries.register: neutral; a staple of news writing and completely at home in speech
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns naming events, people, or arrivals — a wave of layoffs, a wave of immigrants, a wave of protests — and, just as commonly, abstract uncountable nouns naming a feeling that comes over someone: a wave of relief, a wave of nausea, a wave of nostalgia. It does not quantify ordinary masses: ✗ a wave of money is odd, and a wave of water is literal rather than quantitative.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a wave layoffs. It stays before another determiner: a wave of the same complaints.
entries.pattern: a wave of [plural countable] · a wave of [abstract mass] · waves of [noun] · the first / next / latest wave of [noun] · a fresh wave of [noun] · a flurry of [noun]
entries.contrast: A wave of is a quantity with a shape in time: the things arrive together, crest, and pass, and another wave may follow. That is what separates it from a lot of, which is flat, and from a series of, which is a line rather than a surge. Its short-lived cousin a flurry of names a brief scattered burst — a flurry of emails, a flurry of activity — and cannot describe anything sustained; a spate of insists the burst was sudden and usually unwelcome; a surge of is the same shape without the falling half. Agreement follows the head in practice: A wave of layoffs is coming keeps the singular, while Waves of protesters were arriving is plural.
entries.variants: a flurry of, waves of, a fresh wave of, a surge of, a spate of, a rash of
entries.see also: a series of, a slew of, a host of, droves of, a bevy of

entries.meaning: ✗ With of: of is obligatory in this plural quantifier — ✗ dozens emails. The exact numeral behaves in the opposite way: after a number, dozen is ✗ singular and takes no of — two dozen eggs, three dozen roses. ✗ two dozens of eggs breaks both halves of the rule at once. Names an indefinite number in the tens, offered as a large one.
examples: Dozens of people were waiting outside before the doors opened.
She sent dozens of emails and got two replies.
Dozens of flights were canceled up and down the coast.
We found dozens of the same typo scattered through the manuscript.
He must have watched that movie dozens of times.
I picked up two dozen eggs on the way home.
entries.русский: десятки — неопределённо много, счёт на десятки
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — dozens of emails, dozens of people. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ dozens of information, ✗ dozens of furniture, ✗ dozens of money. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.pattern: dozens of [plural countable] · dozens of [the/these + plural] · dozens upon dozens of [plural] · compare [number] dozen [plural noun]
entries.contrast: This is the governing rule for the whole dozen / hundred / thousand / million family: ✗ after a number, singular and no of (two dozen, three hundred, five thousand); ✗ alone as a quantifier, plural and of required (dozens of, hundreds of, thousands of). Dozens of claims an indefinite number in the tens — more than a handful, fewer than a hundred — and no one is expected to have counted. The one place the numeral and the quantifier meet is a dozen, which means exactly twelve except in the loose idiom a dozen times. Bare dozens is also a pronoun, with the of-phrase left understood: Dozens were turned away at the door.
entries.variants: dozens upon dozens of, several dozen, a dozen, half a dozen
entries.see also: hundreds of, thousands of, scores of, dozen, hundred, thousand, million, billion

entries.meaning: Names a large number of people or animals moving together in one direction.
examples: Droves of tourists come through the canyon between May and September.
Subscribers canceled in droves after the price increase.
Droves of young families have moved into the county since the plant opened.
Volunteers turned out in droves for the first cleanup and in twos for every one after it.
Droves of voters skipped the primary altogether.
The road was closed for a drove of cattle crossing to the summer pasture.
entries.русский: толпы, валом — о людях или животных, движущихся массой
entries.register: neutral to informal and mildly vivid; common in journalism, since the word still pictures livestock being driven along a road
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns naming people or animals only — droves of tourists, droves of voters, droves of cattle. Never an uncountable noun (✗ droves of money) and, in careful use, never inanimate things: ✗ droves of emails reads as a mixed metaphor.
entries.with of: of is obligatory in the determiner use — ✗ droves tourists. The far commoner construction is the adverbial in droves, which takes no noun at all and modifies the verb — They left in droves — and is a prepositional phrase, not a determiner: it cannot be moved in front of a noun (✗ in droves people left). The singular a drove of survives mainly for livestock.
entries.pattern: droves of [plural animate] · droves of [the + plural] · [verb] + in droves (adverbial) · a drove of [livestock]
entries.contrast: Droves of and in droves are one word doing two jobs, and only the first is a determiner. Both carry the same picture — a herd moving in one direction — and both are usually about people behaving as a mass: subscribers canceled in droves. Against hordes of, which adds disorder and a faint hostility, and against masses of, which is shapeless, droves of implies movement with a direction. Unlike dozens, hundreds, and thousands, bare droves is not used as a pronoun: ✗ Droves were turned away.
entries.variants: in droves, a drove of, throngs of, hordes of
entries.see also: hordes of, masses of, a bevy of, thousands of, scores of

entries.meaning: Names a large, disorderly crowd of people or animals, with the speaker's disapproval built into the word.
examples: Hordes of shoppers were already in line when the doors opened.
A horde of reporters was waiting on the courthouse steps.
Hordes of mosquitoes came off the marsh at dusk.
The trail is quiet in April and overrun by hordes of day hikers in July.
Hordes of the summer people arrive the week after Memorial Day.
She had pictured a quiet museum morning and walked into a horde of fourth-graders.
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of hoards (stockpiles); the two spellings are not interchangeable
entries.русский: полчища, орды — неодобр.: большая беспорядочная толпа
entries.register: informal to journalistic; vivid and mildly disapproving — the crowd it names is one the speaker would rather avoid
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns naming people or animals — hordes of shoppers, hordes of tourists, hordes of mosquitoes. Never an uncountable noun (✗ hordes of traffic) and not naturally used of inanimate objects (✗ hordes of emails).
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ hordes tourists. The singular a horde of is equally common and means the same thing: a horde of reporters. Bare hordes works as a pronoun only in headline style: Hordes descended on the outlet mall.
entries.pattern: hordes of [plural animate] · a horde of [plural animate] · hordes of [the + plural] · a whole horde of [plural]
entries.contrast: Horde came into English as the name of a Mongol army and never lost the connotation: the crowd is large, unruly, and unwelcome. That built-in judgment is the reason to choose it over neutral crowds of or throngs of, and the reason not to use it of the people you are writing for. Against droves of, which moves in a direction, and masses of, which is shapeless and British-flavored. One spelling warning: horde is a crowd, hoard is a stash, and ✗ hoards of tourists is a common and conspicuous error.
entries.variants: a horde of, a whole horde of, throngs of, swarms of, droves of
entries.see also: droves of, masses of, a bevy of, thousands of, a multitude of

entries.meaning: ✗ With of: of is obligatory — ✗ hundreds people. The exact numeral takes the opposite treatment: after a number, hundred stays ✗ singular with no of — three hundred people, ✗ three hundreds of people. Names an indefinite number in the hundreds, presented as a large one.
examples: Hundreds of people lined up before the store opened.
The repair is going to cost hundreds of dollars.
Hundreds of the letters were returned undelivered.
She drove hundreds of miles out of her way to avoid the interstate.
Hundreds of thousands of households lost power in the storm.
There were three hundred seats and twice that many people.
entries.русский: сотни — неопределённо много, счёт на сотни
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — hundreds of people, hundreds of dollars, hundreds of miles. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ hundreds of money, ✗ hundreds of water. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.pattern: hundreds of [plural countable] · hundreds of [the/these + plural] · hundreds and hundreds of [plural] · hundreds of thousands of [plural] · compare [number] hundred [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Same alternation as dozens of and thousands of: plural plus of for the vague quantity, singular and bare after an exact number. Hundreds of is genuinely vague — it covers anything from about two hundred to just under a thousand, and speakers reach for it precisely because they have not counted. The stacked form hundreds of thousands of is standard and means what it says; each of is required. Bare hundreds is a pronoun in the same way as dozens and thousands: Hundreds were still waiting at midnight.
entries.variants: hundreds and hundreds of, several hundred, hundreds of thousands of, a hundred
entries.see also: dozens of, thousands of, millions of, scores of, hundred, thousand, million, billion, countless

entries.meaning: ✗ With of: of is obligatory — ✗ millions people. After an exact number the word goes ✗ singular and takes no of: two million people, ✗ two millions of people. Billions of behaves identically (three billion dollars, billions of dollars). Names an indefinite number in the millions — and, loosely, any number the speaker wants to call enormous.
examples: Millions of people watched the hearing live.
The cleanup has already cost millions of dollars.
These formations took millions of years to build up.
Millions of the old accounts were never closed out.
I've told him that a million times.
The company employs two million people worldwide.
entries.pronunciation note: of is unstressed and commonly reduces to /ə/
entries.русский: миллионы — букв.; в гиперболе разг. «уйма, тьма»
entries.register: neutral in the literal sense; informal and hyperbolic in the millions of times sense
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — millions of people, millions of dollars, millions of years. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ millions of money, ✗ millions of information, ✗ millions of traffic. Never a bare singular countable noun.
