entries.pattern: millions of [plural countable] · millions of [the/these + plural] · millions upon millions of [plural] · tens of millions of [plural] · compare [number] million [plural noun]
entries.contrast: The top of the dozen / hundred / thousand / million series, obeying the same alternation as the rest of it: plural plus of for a vague quantity, singular and bare after an exact figure. Two of its uses are not counts at all — the plain hyperbole of millions of times and the singular a million in I have a million things to do, which reports exasperation rather than a number and belongs with a zillion and umpteen. Agreement is plural when the phrase counts things (Millions of ballots were mailed) but singular when a figure names one sum or one span (Two million dollars is a lot to write off). Bare millions is also a pronoun: Millions were watching.
entries.variants: millions upon millions of, tens of millions of, billions of, several million, a million (hyperbolic)
entries.see also: thousands of, hundreds of, dozens of, hundred, thousand, million, billion, countless

entries.meaning: Names a large number of countable things — noticeably more than the listener might expect, with a hint that the speaker was mildly surprised too.
examples: Quite a few people asked about that after the meeting.
I've been there quite a few times over the years.
Quite a few of the guests stayed past midnight.
There are quite a few things wrong with that argument.
Quite a few of them had driven in from out of state.
We still have quite a few more boxes to unpack.
entries.русский: немало, порядочно — с исчисляемыми: больше, чем можно было ожидать
entries.register: neutral to informal; very common in American speech and unremarkable in writing
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — quite a few people, quite a few times. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ quite a few money, ✗ quite a few advice. The uncountable partner is quite a bit of.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — quite a few of the guests, quite a few of them. No of before a bare plural: quite a few guests.
entries.pattern: quite a few [plural countable] · quite a few of [the/my/these + plural] · quite a few of [them/us] · quite a few more [plural] · quite a few (pronoun: Quite a few showed up)
entries.contrast: It contains few and it means many. A few people came reports a small number; quite a few people came reports a large one. The same reversal runs through quite a bit of, which means a large amount despite containing a bit. There is no way to derive this from the parts, and the reliable fix is to file quite a few and quite a bit of as unanalyzable single words meaning "a lot." Its uncountable partner is quite a bit of; the merely-small versions are a few and a bit of.
entries.variants: quite a bit of, quite a number of, quite a lot of, quite a few more
entries.see also: quite a bit of, many, quite a lot of, a good many, a few, a bit of, several

entries.meaning: Names an indefinite number in the dozens, in a raised journalistic or literary register.
examples: Scores of protesters gathered outside the statehouse.
Scores of people were treated for smoke inhalation.
The storm downed scores of trees along the river road.
Scores of the letters have never been published.
He has advised scores of first-time candidates.
Scores of small towns lost their only pharmacy in a decade.
entries.русский: десятки — книжн./журн., счёт на дюжины, почти всегда о людях
entries.register: literary and journalistic; slightly elevated and almost always about people or events
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — scores of protesters, scores of injuries. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ scores of damage. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ scores protesters. As an exact numeral, score means twenty and stays singular with no of, but that use is archaic and survives mainly in the biblical three score and ten and in Lincoln's four score and seven years ago.
entries.pattern: scores of [plural countable] · scores of [the + plural] · scores upon scores of [plural] · compare archaic [number] score
entries.contrast: Same family rule as dozens of and hundreds of: plural plus of for a vague quantity. In implied size scores of sits between dozens of and hundreds of, though the arithmetic (a score is twenty) is dead and nobody is really counting. Its register sets it apart from the rest of the family — a news bulletin says scores of people were injured, but nobody says it at the kitchen table. Bare scores is a pronoun in that same headline register (Scores were injured). Do not confuse it with the ordinary noun score, a tally or a piece of written music.
entries.variants: scores upon scores of, three score and ten (archaic), a score of
entries.see also: dozens of, hundreds of, thousands of, a multitude of

entries.meaning: ✗ With of: of is obligatory — ✗ thousands people. After an exact number, thousand is ✗ singular with no of: five thousand people, ✗ five thousands of people. Names an indefinite number in the thousands, presented as a very large one.
examples: Thousands of people were still without power on Thursday.
The repair will run into thousands of dollars.
Tens of thousands of ballots had to be recounted by hand.
These rocks are thousands of years old.
Thousands of the accounts turned out to be automated.
The company laid off five thousand workers in a single quarter.
entries.русский: тысячи — неопределённо много, счёт на тысячи
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — thousands of people, thousands of dollars, thousands of years. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ thousands of money, ✗ thousands of traffic. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.pattern: thousands of [plural countable] · thousands of [the/these + plural] · tens of thousands of [plural] · hundreds of thousands of [plural] · compare [number] thousand [plural noun]
entries.contrast: The last member of the dozen / hundred / thousand family, with the same alternation: plural plus of when the number is vague, singular and bare after an exact figure. The stacked forms are standard and productive — tens of thousands of, hundreds of thousands of, and on up to millions of and billions of, each keeping its own of. American English also uses thousands alone as a pronoun (Thousands were left without water).
entries.variants: tens of thousands of, hundreds of thousands of, millions of, billions of, several thousand
entries.see also: hundreds of, millions of, dozens of, hundred, thousand, million, billion, countless, a large number of

entries.meaning: Names a comically large and deliberately uncounted number of countable things — "I have lost count, and I resent having to."
examples: I've told him umpteen times not to park there.
There were umpteen forms to fill out before anyone would look at the application.
She has been through umpteen rounds of interviews for that job.
We tried umpteen different passwords before the lock finally opened.
The umpteen meetings this quarter have eaten the whole schedule.
For the umpteenth time, the meeting is at nine.
entries.русский: невесть сколько, сто раз — разг., шутливо-раздражённое «сбился со счёта»
entries.position: central, in the numeral slot; like a numeral it is also a postdeterminer after a central determiner — the umpteen forms they made us sign, his umpteen cousins
entries.register: informal and exasperated; current in speech, out of place in formal writing
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — umpteen times, umpteen forms, umpteen reasons. Never an uncountable noun (✗ umpteen money, ✗ umpteen advice) and never a singular countable noun (✗ umpteen excuse), because it behaves grammatically as a plural number word.
entries.with of: no of before a bare noun — umpteen times, never ✗ umpteen of times. The partitive umpteen of the forms is possible on the numeral pattern but rare; speakers say umpteen forms.
entries.pattern: umpteen [plural countable] · [the/his/my] umpteen [plural countable] · for the umpteenth time (the ordinal, far commoner)
entries.contrast: Umpteen is a joke numeral, built from the -teen of thirteen and nineteen on a placeholder ump- out of old military slang. It names a number the speaker refuses to count and always carries impatience: I've told you umpteen times is a complaint, not a statistic. The ordinal umpteenth is by far the commoner form and lives with the numerals. Neutral equivalents are many, countless, and any number of. Note that the related coinages zillion, gazillion, and bazillion pattern on million instead and require an article: a zillion emails, never ✗ zillion emails.
entries.variants: umpteenth, for the umpteenth time, umpty-ump, a zillion, a gazillion, a bazillion
entries.see also: nth, umpteenth, countless, many, dozens of, any amount of

entries.meaning: Describes a supply that is large and easily had. Unlike the of-phrases in this file, it modifies the noun rather than heading its own phrase, which is why it can stack with a determiner: their abundant natural resources.
examples: There is abundant evidence that the practice continued for years.
The region has abundant sunshine and almost no rain.
Abundant parking is the one thing that mall got right.
Wildflowers were abundant along the whole ridge.
The county's abundant water rights turned out to be worth more than the land.
The archive contains an abundance of material nobody has read.
entries.русский: обильный, изобильный — прилагательное: много и легко доступно
entries.position: attributive (abundant evidence, the abundant wildlife) or predicative (rainfall was abundant that spring)
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in science and nature writing
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (abundant evidence, abundant sunshine, abundant rainfall) and plural countable nouns (abundant resources, abundant opportunities). With a singular countable noun it needs an article and reads oddly unless the noun is mass-like: an abundant harvest works, ✗ an abundant chair does not.
entries.with of: the adjective takes no of-phrase — ✗ abundant of evidence. The noun it is built on does: an abundance of evidence, an abundance of options, and that phrase is a full partitive quantifier.
entries.pattern: abundant [uncountable/plural countable] · [the/his] abundant [noun] · [noun] is abundant · an abundance of [noun] · abundantly [adjective/verb]
entries.contrast: Three neighbors, three different claims. Abundant says the supply is large and freely available; ample says it is large enough for the purpose; plentiful is the plain everyday word for what abundant says formally. Because it is an adjective it can be graded (more abundant, most abundant) and can follow a determiner (the abundant evidence) — two things no real determiner can do, and the quickest way to prove it is not one. The small-quantity opposites are scarce and sparse.
entries.variants: plentiful, an abundance of, abundantly, superabundant, in abundance
entries.see also: ample, copious, a wealth of, plenty of, sparse

entries.meaning: Describes a quantity that is large enough for the purpose with room left over.
examples: There's ample time to catch the connecting flight.
The lot has ample parking even on a game day.
They were given ample warning that the deadline would not move.
There is ample evidence in the record to support the ruling.
The grant gave her ample opportunities to travel.
His patience was amply rewarded.
entries.русский: достаточный с запасом, обильный — хватает на всё и ещё остаётся
entries.position: attributive almost always (ample time, ample parking, the ample evidence); predicative use is possible but stiff
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (ample time, ample evidence, ample room, ample warning) and plural countable nouns (ample opportunities, ample supplies). With a singular countable it takes an article and shifts toward the physical sense of "roomy": an ample kitchen.
entries.with of: takes no of-phrase — ✗ ample of time. The idea is expressed instead by plenty of or an abundance of.
entries.pattern: ample [uncountable/plural countable] · [the/his] ample [noun] · more than ample [noun] · amply [past participle] (amply rewarded)
entries.contrast: Ample is plenty of in one word: it does not merely report a large quantity, it certifies that the quantity is enough and to spare. That sufficiency is what separates it from abundant (large supply, no promise about need) and from sufficient (exactly enough, nothing spare). Note the second, physical sense — an ample kitchen, ample proportions — where the word means spacious rather than numerous, and be aware that applied to a person's body it is a dated euphemism.
entries.variants: more than ample, amply, ampleness, plenty of
entries.see also: plenty of, enough, sufficient, abundant, a wealth of

entries.meaning: Describes a large amount of something uncountable, in the register a report or a ruling uses.
examples: The storm did considerable damage to the pier.
She has considerable experience in labor arbitration.
It took considerable time to reconstruct the records.
The considerable expense of the repair was never in the budget.
They committed considerable resources to a project nobody wanted.
The second draft is considerably better than the first.
entries.pronunciation note: the first syllable is unstressed and reduced, /kən/, never /kɑn/
entries.русский: значительный, немалый — книжн., с неисчисляемыми
entries.position: attributive (considerable damage, the considerable expense) or predicative (the damage was considerable)
entries.register: formal to neutral — the written stand-in for a lot of in front of a mass noun; in speech Americans say a lot of
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns above all — considerable time, considerable damage, considerable expense, considerable evidence, considerable experience. It reaches plural countable nouns only when the plural names an aggregate or an abstract quantity rather than a set of individual objects — considerable resources, considerable sums, considerable delays, considerable difficulties are all standard, while ordinary concrete plurals are not: ✗ considerable chairs, ✗ considerable emails, where the word you want is numerous or a lot of. With a singular countable noun it takes an article and shifts from "much" to "large": a considerable sum, a considerable distance.
entries.with of: takes no of-phrase — ✗ considerable of the damage. To pick a part out of a determined phrase you must switch words: much of the damage, a good deal of the damage. The fixed phrase of considerable + noun exists as a formal predicate (a matter of considerable importance).
entries.pattern: considerable [uncountable] · [the/his] considerable [uncountable] · a considerable [singular noun of measure] · considerable numbers / amounts of [noun] · considerably [comparative] (considerably worse)
entries.contrast: Considerable is the mass half of the formal pair whose count half is numerous: considerable damage beside numerous complaints, and neither will take the other's noun. Against substantial, which suggests solidity and is the word for sums and meals; against significant, which in careful writing claims importance rather than size — a significant delay matters, a considerable delay is merely long. Being an adjective it follows a determiner (the considerable expense), stands after the verb (the damage was considerable), and has a degree adverb of its own (considerably better) — three things no determiner in this file can do.
entries.variants: considerably, substantial, significant, appreciable, of considerable [noun]
entries.see also: numerous, a great deal of, much, ample, abundant

entries.meaning: Describes something produced or supplied in great volume.
examples: She took copious notes throughout the deposition.
The season brought copious rainfall to the valley.
He left behind copious correspondence with three separate publishers.
The recipe calls for copious amounts of butter.
The manuscript is annotated copiously in two different hands.
Copious footnotes do not make an argument sound.
entries.русский: обильный, в большом объёме — книжн.
entries.position: attributive (copious notes, her copious correspondence); predicative is rare and bookish
entries.register: formal and slightly literary; in speech Americans say tons of or a lot of
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (copious rainfall, copious bleeding) and plural countable nouns (copious notes, copious footnotes). It is unusually collocation-bound: copious notes, copious amounts of, and copious quantities of account for most real uses.
entries.with of: takes no of-phrase of its own — ✗ copious of notes — but it very often modifies one: copious amounts of coffee, copious quantities of data.
entries.pattern: copious [uncountable/plural countable] · [her/the] copious [noun] · copious amounts of [uncountable] · copiously (adverb)
entries.contrast: Where abundant describes a supply that is there for the taking, copious describes output — what something produces or emits in volume: notes, tears, rainfall, bleeding, correspondence. That is why copious notes is idiomatic and copious parking is not. Its Latin root is the same as copy and cornucopia, and the register it carries is bookish enough that the phrase copious amounts of often reads as mild self-parody.
entries.variants: copiously, copious amounts of, copious quantities of, voluminous
entries.see also: abundant, a wealth of, ample, masses of

entries.meaning: Describes a number so large the speaker will not attempt it — an emphatic many rather than an estimate.
examples: She has explained this countless times to countless people.
Countless hours went into cleaning up that database.
The bridge has been photographed by countless tourists.
Countless small decisions add up to a house that doesn't work.
He rewrote the opening paragraph countless times.
The storm caused untold damage along the coast.
entries.русский: бесчисленный, несчётный — эмфатическое many, а не оценка
entries.position: attributive only (countless times, the countless small decisions); it has no predicative use — ✗ the errors were countless is at best strained
entries.register: neutral, with a rhetorical lift; fine in speech and in writing
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — countless times, countless hours, countless people. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ countless information, ✗ countless money, ✗ countless damage. The word literally means "too many to count," so it needs something countable to fail to count.
entries.with of: takes no of-phrase — ✗ countless of the applicants. Before a determined phrase you need a different word: many of the applicants, any number of the applicants.
entries.pattern: countless [plural countable] · [the/his] countless [plural noun] · countless times / countless hours (the two commonest collocations)
entries.contrast: Countless is a rhetorical many: it does not report a number, it announces that the speaker declines to. Innumerable is its formal twin, and untold is the one to reach for with uncountables, since untold damage and untold wealth are idiomatic where ✗ countless damage is not. The informal equivalent is umpteen, and the hyperbolic ones are a million and a zillion.
entries.variants: innumerable, numberless, untold (with uncountables), uncounted
entries.see also: numerous, myriad, umpteen, thousands of, many

entries.meaning: Describes a great and varied number of countable things.
examples: The city faces myriad problems and has money for about three of them.
There are a myriad of ways to configure the thing, all badly documented.
Myriad small streams feed into the reservoir.
Her essays touch on a myriad of subjects.
The reef supports myriad species found nowhere else.
Myriads of insects rose off the water at dusk.
entries.русский: мириады, несметное множество — книжн.: много и разного
entries.position: attributive with no article at all (myriad problems) or as the head of a partitive phrase (a myriad of problems)
entries.register: formal or literary in both constructions
entries.type: adjective and noun with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns in both patterns — myriad options, a myriad of options. Uncountable use is rare and reads as a stretch (myriad information is odd). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: the two constructions split on exactly this point. Bare myriad takes no of — myriad reasons, ✗ myriad of reasons without an article. The noun construction requires both an article and of — a myriad of reasons. Both are standard, despite a long-lived complaint that the of version is an error; the noun use is in fact the older of the two by centuries.
entries.pattern: myriad [plural countable] · a myriad of [plural countable] · myriads of [plural countable] · [the/her] myriad [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Myriad was Greek for exactly ten thousand and now means simply "very many," usually with a note of variety built in: myriad options suggests not just a lot of options but a lot of different kinds. Against countless, which stresses that counting is hopeless, myriad stresses that the set is diverse. The only live usage question is of, and the answer is that both forms are correct so long as the article and the of travel together.
entries.variants: a myriad of, myriads of, manifold, multifarious
entries.see also: countless, numerous, a multitude of, a plethora of, many

entries.meaning: Describes a large number of countable things, in a formal register.
examples: The agency received numerous complaints about the same contractor.
He has been warned on numerous occasions.
Numerous studies have failed to replicate the original finding.
Her objections were numerous and, as it turned out, correct.
The bill contains numerous exemptions added late in the session.
Small farms are far more numerous there than the statistics suggest.
entries.русский: многочисленный — книжн. замена many
entries.position: attributive (numerous errors, his numerous absences) or predicative (the errors were numerous)
entries.register: formal — the written stand-in for many in reports, legal writing, and journalism
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — numerous complaints, numerous occasions, numerous studies. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ numerous information, ✗ numerous evidence, ✗ numerous progress. For uncountables the formal equivalents are much, considerable, and a great deal of.
entries.with of: takes no of-phrase in standard American usage — ✗ numerous of the students. To pick a subset out of a determined phrase you must switch words: many of the students, a large number of the students.
entries.pattern: numerous [plural countable] · [his/the] numerous [plural noun] · [plural noun] are numerous · more numerous than [phrase] · on numerous occasions
entries.contrast: Numerous is many in a suit, and the differences are grammatical, not semantic. It is an adjective, so it follows a determiner (his numerous absences), grades and compares (more numerous, most numerous), and stands after the verb (the objections were numerous) — none of which many does in the same way, and many in turn heads an of-phrase that numerous cannot. It counts only, which rules out ✗ numerous evidence, and its register rules it out of casual speech: nobody says I got numerous emails at lunch.
entries.variants: more numerous, on numerous occasions, numerously (rare), innumerable
entries.see also: many, considerable, countless, a large number of, a great many, several

entries.meaning: Marks a quantity that meets the need exactly — as much or as many as is required, and no claim beyond that. Under negation it becomes the standard way to report a shortfall: not enough chairs, not enough time.
examples: Do we have enough chairs for everyone?
There isn't enough coffee left for a second round.
He's finally saved enough money for the deposit.
I've had enough of these delays.
Is it warm enough out there for the porch?
There's time enough to fix it before Monday.
entries.pronunciation note: carefully /ɪˈnʌf/; the first syllable is always reduced, never /iː/
entries.русский: достаточно, хватает — ровно столько, сколько нужно; not enough — не хватает
entries.position: central determiner before the noun (enough time); in formal and fixed usage it may also follow the noun (time enough, reason enough, money enough), which no other determiner in English can do; as a degree adverb it follows its adjective (good enough)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (enough chairs, enough volunteers) and uncountable nouns (enough time, enough money). Not used with a bare singular countable noun (✗ enough chair).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — enough of the food, enough of my time, enough of this, enough of them. No of before a bare noun: enough food.
entries.pattern: enough [plural/uncountable] · [noun] enough (formal/fixed) · enough of [the/my/this + noun] · enough of [them/it] · [adjective/adverb] + enough · enough to [verb] · not enough [noun]
entries.contrast: Enough names the sufficiency line itself: below it are not enough, too few, and too little; above it are too many and too much; comfortably above it are plenty of and ample. Two structural oddities are worth memorizing. First, as a degree word it follows what it modifies — warm enough, quickly enough, never ✗ enough warm — which is the reverse of very, too, and so. Second, it is the only determiner that can trail its own noun in standard English (There's time enough for that), a survival of older word order now limited to a handful of nouns. As a pronoun it stands alone: That's enough.
entries.variants: not enough, more than enough, enough to, enough of, sure enough, oddly enough, fair enough, enough is enough
entries.see also: sufficient, plenty of, ample, much, not much, little, enow

entries.meaning: Describes an amount or number that meets a stated requirement — the formal register's enough.
examples: The court found sufficient evidence to send the case to trial.
The account did not have sufficient funds to cover the check.
Allow sufficient time for the adhesive to cure.
Two witnesses were deemed sufficient.
There were insufficient grounds for a second search.
The lighting was sufficient for reading but not for close work.
entries.русский: достаточный — книжн./юр. вариант enough
entries.position: attributive (sufficient evidence, sufficient funds) or predicative (the evidence was sufficient)
entries.register: formal — legal, medical, financial, and academic writing; in speech Americans say enough
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (sufficient evidence, sufficient time, sufficient cause) and plural countable nouns (sufficient funds, sufficient resources, sufficient grounds). Not used with a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: takes no of-phrase — ✗ sufficient of the evidence; the repair is enough of the evidence. The abstract noun a sufficiency of exists but is rare and archaic.
entries.pattern: sufficient [uncountable/plural countable] · [the] sufficient [noun] · [noun] is sufficient · sufficient to [verb] · sufficient for [noun] · insufficient [noun]
entries.contrast: Sufficient is the formal enough, and the grammar is where they part. Sufficient is an ordinary adjective: it goes before the noun only (✗ evidence sufficient outside legal set phrases), it cannot modify another adjective (✗ sufficient warm — warm enough), and it has a standard negative twin, insufficient, where enough has to borrow not. Note also the technical sense from logic and mathematics — a sufficient condition is one that guarantees a result, which has nothing to do with quantity. Adequate sits between the two: like sufficient it is formal, but it hints that the amount only barely meets the need.
entries.variants: insufficient, adequate, sufficiently, a sufficiency of (archaic), self-sufficient
entries.see also: enough, ample, plenty of, abundant

entries.meaning: Names a large quantity of anything, countable or not, in an informal and distinctly American register with a rural edge.
examples: That boy is in a whole heap of trouble.
It'd cost a heap of money to put a new roof on that barn.
We've got a heap of work to do before the inspector comes.
A heap of folks around here still heat with wood.
She's forgotten a heap of things she used to know by heart.
There was a heap of laundry on the bed and nowhere to sit down.
entries.pronunciation note: in casual speech of reduces to /ə/: /ə ˈhipə/, "a heapa trouble"
entries.русский: куча, уйма — разг. амер. с южным, деревенским оттенком
entries.register: informal American with a Southern and rural flavor — ordinary in speech across the South and the lower Midwest, common in country lyrics and in reported dialect, and out of place in formal writing. It is the domestic singular and is not the same animal as the Australian and British plural heaps of
entries.goes with: both uncountable nouns (a heap of trouble, a heap of money, a heap of work) and plural countable nouns (a heap of problems, a heap of folks). The literal sense is an ordinary noun and pluralizes freely: a heap of laundry, two heaps of gravel. Never a bare singular countable noun: ✗ a heap of chair.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a heap trouble. Bare a heap is an adverb in the same register (I like it a heap, a heap better), which is regional and dated and not a determiner.
entries.pattern: a heap of [uncountable] · a heap of [plural countable] · a whole heap of [noun] · a heap (regional adverb: a heap better) · compare heaps of (Australian and British)
entries.contrast: The singular a heap of is American and Southern-flavored; the plural heaps of is Australian and British and sounds imported in the United States — the same word split by an ocean. The intensified a whole heap of is the commoner of the two in speech and is almost always about trouble: you are in a whole heap of trouble is close to a fixed phrase. The neutral equivalents are a lot of and a great deal of; the vulgar one is a shitload of. Agreement follows the noun after of: A heap of people were waiting, A heap of work is left.
entries.variants: a whole heap of, heaps of, a heap (regional adverb), a pile of, a mountain of
entries.see also: heaps of, tons of, a mess of, a passel of, a lot of

entries.meaning: Names a large quantity of anything, countable or not, in casual non-American speech.
examples: There's heaps of room in the back if you want to stretch out.
She's got heaps of experience with this kind of client.
Heaps of people turned up for the first session.
We've still got heaps of time before the ferry.
He brought heaps of food, most of which went home again.
There was a heap of laundry on the bed.
entries.русский: куча, полно — разг., преим. брит./австрал.; амер. аналог tons of
entries.register: informal; chiefly Australian, New Zealand, and British. Americans understand it and read it as foreign — the domestic equivalent is tons of
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (heaps of people) and uncountable nouns (heaps of time, heaps of room). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory before a noun — ✗ heaps people. Bare heaps is a pronoun or adverb in the same dialects (Thanks heaps, heaps better), and that use does not travel to American English at all.
entries.pattern: heaps of [plural/uncountable] · heaps of [the/my + noun] · heaps (pronoun/adverb, non-American)
entries.contrast: The literal a heap of — a physical pile — still exists (a heap of laundry), and the quantifier is its bleached descendant, exactly as a pile of, a mountain of, and a stack of are heading the same way. Within the informal group, heaps of and loads of are interchangeable in the dialects that use them; the American reflexes are tons of and a bunch of. Agreement follows the noun after of.
entries.variants: a heap of, heaps (adverb), loads of, tons of
entries.see also: a heap of, tons of, loads of, masses of, lots of, a bunch of

entries.meaning: Names a large casual quantity of anything, countable or not.
examples: We've got loads of time before the show starts.
Loads of people said the same thing on the way out.
She has loads of patience with the new hires.
There were loads of the little green ones and none of the red.
That project ate loads of money and produced nothing.
He talked for an hour and it was a load of nonsense.
entries.русский: куча, масса — разг., брит. по происхождению, но понятно и в США
entries.register: informal; British-leaning but widely used and fully understood in the United States
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (loads of people) and uncountable nouns (loads of money, loads of time). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory before a noun — ✗ loads people. Bare loads is a pronoun (We've got loads) and, in British usage, an adverb (loads better), which Americans generally avoid.
entries.pattern: loads of [plural/uncountable] · loads of [the/my + noun] · loads of [them/it] · a load of [noun] (often dismissive: a load of nonsense)
entries.contrast: Loads of and lots of differ only in bulk of imagery, and both are one step below a lot of in formality. The singular a load of has drifted somewhere else entirely: it is usually dismissive (a load of nonsense, a load of trouble) rather than merely quantitative. Agreement follows the noun after of: Loads of people are coming, Loads of work is left.
entries.variants: a load of, loads (adverb, British), lots of, tons of
entries.see also: lots of, tons of, heaps of, masses of, a lot of

entries.meaning: Names a large, shapeless quantity of anything, countable or not.
examples: There were masses of people on the platform by seven.
The move generated masses of paperwork.
She has masses of material she has never published.
Masses of the old records were destroyed in the flood.
He came home with masses of photographs and no notes.
The wall behind the rack was a mass of unlabeled wires.
entries.русский: масса, уйма — разг., преим. брит.
entries.register: informal; chiefly British, understood but uncommon in American speech
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (masses of people) and uncountable nouns (masses of paperwork, masses of data). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory before a noun — ✗ masses people. Bare masses is an ordinary plural noun (the masses, meaning ordinary people), not a quantifier.
entries.pattern: masses of [plural/uncountable] · masses of [the/my + noun] · a mass of [uncountable/plural]
entries.contrast: Masses of stresses undifferentiated bulk — the quantity is large and shapeless, which is why it suits paperwork, data, and crowds. The singular a mass of is more common in American English and can be neutral or faintly negative (a mass of contradictions, a mass of wires). Do not read the masses as a quantifier: it is a plain noun phrase meaning ordinary people.
entries.variants: a mass of, masses (pronoun), loads of, heaps of
entries.see also: loads of, heaps of, tons of, copious, a lot of

entries.meaning: Names a large and seemingly inexhaustible quantity — most often of trouble, and occasionally of pleasure.
examples: That one clause caused us no end of trouble.
The kids had no end of fun with the box the couch came in.
He's given the department no end of headaches.
There is no end of advice available and very little of it useful.
No end of people have offered to help and none have shown up.
The promotion pleased her no end.
entries.русский: уйма, конца-краю нет — чаще о неприятностях
entries.register: informal to conversational; slightly old-fashioned but alive
entries.goes with: both uncountable nouns (no end of trouble, no end of fun) and plural countable nouns (no end of problems, no end of excuses). It strongly favors abstract nouns naming trouble or pleasure; it is odd with concrete objects (✗ no end of chairs).
entries.with of: of is obligatory and cannot be dropped — ✗ no end trouble. Note that the no attaches to end, not to the noun after of, which is why the phrase is not a negative.
entries.pattern: no end of [uncountable] · no end of [plural countable] · cause/give/have no end of [noun] · no end (adverb: it pleased her no end)
entries.contrast: It contains no and it means "a great deal of." That gave us no end of trouble means a great deal of trouble, not none: the no negates end, so the phrase says the trouble was endless. Because it is positive in quantity it does not license negative polarity items — no end of trouble at all is odd where no trouble at all is fine. It is the mirror image of no amount of, which really is negative (No amount of trouble would stop her). The adverb no end is the same idiom (It pleased him no end).
entries.variants: no end (adverb), endless, any amount of, no shortage of
entries.see also: any amount of, countless, tons of, no, a host of

entries.meaning: Names a large and pleasing quantity of anything, in a deliberately light register.
examples: The house has oodles of charm and no insulation.
They gave us oodles of time to get the paperwork in.
She baked oodles of cookies for the bake sale.
There's oodles of room in that back yard for a garden.
He's got oodles of stories about that summer.
Oodles and oodles of people signed up and about half showed.
entries.русский: уйма, навалом — разг., шутливо-умильное
entries.register: informal and jocular; dated-cute, American in origin, used with a wink
entries.goes with: both uncountable nouns (oodles of time, oodles of money) and plural countable nouns (oodles of cookies). It gravitates to pleasant things — time, money, charm, fun — and sounds wrong with unpleasant ones (✗ oodles of debt).
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ oodles time. There is no singular ✗ an oodle; the word exists only in this plural quantifier frame.
entries.pattern: oodles of [uncountable] · oodles of [plural countable] · oodles and oodles of [noun]
entries.contrast: Oodles of is the most self-consciously playful member of the group. Its nearest relatives in tone are scads of, gobs of, and bazillions of, all American and all jocular; the neutral equivalents are plenty of and a lot of. The positive skew is real and is worth noticing: oodles of charm is idiomatic, oodles of trouble is not — for trouble the idiom is no end of.
entries.variants: oodles and oodles of, scads of, gobs of, a boatload of
entries.see also: tons of, loads of, plenty of, a bunch of

entries.meaning: Names a large quantity of anything, countable or not, with no pretense of measurement.
examples: We got tons of email about that segment.
There's tons of parking behind the building.
She's put tons of work into the garden this spring.
Tons of people showed up for the free clinic.
I have a ton of reading to do before Monday.
Thanks — that helped a ton.
entries.русский: куча, вагон, море — разг. амер., главное гиперболическое «много»
entries.register: informal American — the default hyperbolic quantifier in US speech
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (tons of people, tons of emails) and uncountable nouns (tons of money, tons of work, tons of time). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ tons people. The singular a ton of is equally common and equally figurative (a ton of work), and both stay before another determiner: tons of the leftover paint.
entries.pattern: tons of [plural/uncountable] · a ton of [plural/uncountable] · tons of [the/my + noun] · tons of [them/it] · a ton (adverb: it helped a ton)
entries.contrast: This is the American member of the heaps / loads / masses set and by far the most frequent of them in US speech. Nothing about it is literal: tons of time weighs nothing, and the literal use (two tons of gravel) keeps a number in front and stays singular, exactly like the dozen / hundred alternation. Agreement follows the noun after of: Tons of people are coming beside Tons of work is left. Register is the only thing keeping it out of formal writing, where the equivalents are a great deal of and a large number of.
entries.variants: a ton of, a ton (adverb), a metric ton of, a boatload of, a truckload of
entries.see also: a bunch of, loads of, heaps of, lots of, a lot of

entries.meaning: Marks a large and sufficient quantity, tacked onto the end of the noun for effect.
examples: There were reasons aplenty to walk away from that deal.
The estate sale had bargains aplenty and nowhere to park.
That summer brought rain aplenty and not one good tomato.
He has stories aplenty about the years before the mill closed.
The season gave the team trouble aplenty and one memorable night in October.
In the older spelling the fiddler promised music a-plenty and dancing until dawn.
entries.pronunciation note: the first syllable is always the weak /ə/, never /eɪ/; the nt commonly reduces in American speech to /əˈplɛni/, "a-plenny"
entries.русский: в изобилии, хоть отбавляй — книжн., ставится после существительного
entries.position: after the noun it quantifies — reasons aplenty, food aplenty — and never before it: ✗ aplenty reasons. It attaches to a bare noun and brings no determiner slot of its own
entries.register: literary and a little archaic; alive in journalism reaching for a flourish, in sports writing, and in travel and cookbook prose. Nobody says it at a kitchen table. The hyphenated a-plenty is the older spelling and now reads as period or country-music styling
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (reasons aplenty, bargains aplenty) and uncountable nouns (food aplenty, trouble aplenty, rain aplenty). Never a singular countable noun: ✗ a reason aplenty.
entries.with of: it never takes of — ✗ aplenty of food. The of-phrase equivalent is plenty of, which is the same word in the ordinary prenominal position: plenty of food = food aplenty.
entries.pattern: [plural or uncountable noun] + aplenty · there is / there are [noun] aplenty · compare prenominal plenty of [noun]
entries.contrast: Aplenty is plenty of turned around, and the reversal is the whole difference: plenty of food is neutral reporting, food aplenty is a flourish. Its fellow postpositive is galore, which is louder, more jocular, and mostly reserved for welcome things, where aplenty is happy to quantify trouble. Neither may precede its noun and neither takes of. The old spelling a-plenty preserves the a- prefix the word is built on, the same one in afire, asleep, and abed.
entries.variants: a-plenty, plenty of, galore, in plenty
entries.see also: galore, plenty of, enough, ample, a wealth of

entries.meaning: Marks a large and pleasing quantity, tacked onto the end of the noun.
examples: The flyer promised bargains galore and delivered a parking lot of folding tables.
There are opportunities galore for anyone willing to move.
The buffet had shrimp galore and nothing else worth the trip.
October brings tourists, traffic, and pumpkin bread galore.
The rewrite fixed the plot and left us with typos galore.
He came home from the fair with prizes galore and no money.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the second syllable; the first is the weak /ɡə/, never /ɡeɪ/
entries.русский: навалом, в изобилии — разг., шутл.; ставится после существительного
entries.position: after the noun it quantifies — bargains galore, whiskey galore — and never before it: ✗ galore bargains. It attaches to a bare noun and does not combine with a determiner of its own: ✗ the bargains galore
entries.register: informal and jocular; a headline, advertising, menu, and flyer word. Common in American English, but always with a wink — a store advertises savings galore, an annual report does not
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (bargains galore, prizes galore, options galore) and uncountable nouns (fun galore, whiskey galore). Never a singular countable noun: ✗ a prize galore. It strongly prefers welcome things; problems galore is possible but lands as sarcasm.
entries.with of: it never takes of — ✗ galore of bargains. The prenominal equivalents are plenty of, lots of, and tons of.
entries.pattern: [plural or uncountable noun] + galore · there are [noun] galore · compare prenominal lots of / plenty of [noun]
entries.contrast: Galore is the loudest of the postpositives and the only common American quantifier borrowed from Irish — go leor, "enough" — which is also why the stress sits where it does. Against aplenty, which is literary and neutral about what it counts, galore is playful and skews to good news. The rule to memorize is positional: it goes after the noun, and a learner who writes ✗ galore opportunities has made the one error the word invites. Compton Mackenzie's Whisky Galore and the film made from it are where many readers meet the word first.
entries.variants: aplenty, plenty of, lots of, in abundance
entries.see also: aplenty, plenty of, tons of, oodles of, a wealth of

entries.meaning: A large quantity of anything, in Southern and Appalachian speech — and, in the kitchen, as much of something as feeds the table.
examples: He caught a mess of crappie off the dock before breakfast.
Mama cooked a mess of greens and a pan of cornbread.
That truck is going to cost you a whole mess of money.
They've got a mess of grandkids running around that house.
You're fixing to buy yourself a mess of trouble.
There's a mess of paperwork to get through before any of that can happen.
entries.pronunciation note: casually /ə ˈmɛsə/, "a messa"
entries.русский: куча, целая гора — диал. (Юг, Аппалачи); о еде — сколько хватит на стол
entries.register: regional American — Southern, Appalachian, and rural Midwestern. Ordinary in speech there and instantly marked as dialect anywhere else, though it is understood nationally from fiction, film, and food writing
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (a mess of catfish, a mess of kids) and uncountable nouns (a mess of trouble, a mess of money). It has one specialized use that is not a quantifier at all but a food term: a mess of greens, a mess of beans, a mess of fish names as much as gets cooked and put on the table at one meal, and mess there is an ordinary countable noun (two messes of collards). Never a bare singular countable noun: ✗ a mess of chair.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a mess trouble. It stays before another determiner: a mess of the paperwork.
entries.pattern: a mess of [plural countable] · a mess of [uncountable] · a whole mess of [noun] · a mess of [greens / beans / fish] (the food sense)
entries.contrast: Do not read the ordinary noun mess — disorder, a bad state — into the quantifier: a mess of kids means a lot of children, not badly behaved ones, and a whole mess of money is a compliment to the sum. The food sense descends from the same mess as mess hall, a portion served out, and is the older of the two. Within the region a mess of, a passel of, and a heap of are close neighbors; the national equivalents are a bunch of and a lot of.
entries.variants: a whole mess of, a passel of, a heap of, messes of (food sense)
entries.see also: a passel of, a right smart of, a heap of, a sight of, a bunch of

entries.meaning: A large number of countable things — usually children, relatives, or animals — in Appalachian, Southern, and Western American speech.
examples: They came into town with a passel of kids and a truck full of furniture.
There's a whole passel of cousins on her mother's side.
A passel of hound dogs came around the side of the house.
The company sent a passel of lawyers to a hearing that lasted twelve minutes.
He'd been through a passel of jobs before he settled on the mail route.
We've got a passel of work to do before dark.
entries.pronunciation note: casually /ə ˈpæsələ/, "a passela"
entries.русский: куча, орава — диал. амер., обычно о детях, родне или животных
entries.register: regional American — Appalachian, Southern, and Western. It is also a stock ingredient of folksy and frontier writing, where it tends to be laid on thick. Understood nationally, produced regionally, and never neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns above all, and especially people and animals — a passel of kids, a passel of hound dogs, a passel of lawyers. Uncountables occur (a passel of trouble) but the plural is the norm. Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a passel kids. It stays before another determiner: a passel of them.
entries.pattern: a passel of [plural countable] · a whole passel of [plural] · a passel of [the/them + plural]
entries.contrast: Passel is a worn-down pronunciation of parcel, and the two are one word with two histories: the standard spelling kept the contempt and lives on in a parcel of lies, while the dialect spelling kept the quantity and went into American country speech. Its neighbors a mess of and a heap of cover the same ground; what marks a passel of off from them is that it nearly always counts people or animals. Use it in dialogue only, and know that laying it on is the standard tell of a writer imitating a region they did not grow up in.
entries.variants: a whole passel of, a parcel of, a mess of, a slew of
entries.see also: a mess of, a heap of, a right smart of, a parcel of, a bunch of

entries.meaning: A great deal of something uncountable, in older rural American and Irish-descended speech — now chiefly alive in a power of good.
examples: A week at the lake would do you a power of good.
That woman has forgotten a power of things most people never learned.
It took a power of work to get the bottom field cleared that first year.
"He's spent a power of money on that house," she said, "and it still leans."
The rain that spring did a power of good and a fair bit of damage besides.
In today's American English the living version of the phrase is a world of good.
entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /ə/: /ə ˈpaʊɚə/
entries.русский: уйма, страсть сколько — устар./диал.; ныне живо лишь в a power of good
entries.register: dialectal and old-fashioned — Southern and Appalachian American, and the Irish and British country speech the American use descends from. In present-day American English it survives almost entirely inside the fixed phrase a power of good; anything past that reads as period writing or as dialect
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns above all — a power of good, a power of money, a power of trouble, a power of work. Plural countables are rare and strictly dialectal (a power of people). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a power good. Keep it clear of the ordinary noun power taking a complement, where power is the real head and means authority: the power of the press, a power of attorney, the power of the purse.
entries.pattern: do [someone] a power of good (the surviving fixed phrase) · a power of [uncountable] · a power of [the + uncountable]
entries.contrast: The living American equivalent is a world of: it did him a world of good says today what a power of good says in an older or more rural voice. Against its regional neighbors a sight of and a heap of, a power of is the one most likely to have been learned from a grandparent rather than from a neighbor. Do not confuse it with a power of attorney, which is a legal instrument and not a quantity, or with the powers that be.
entries.variants: a power of good, a world of, a sight of, a heap of
entries.see also: a sight of, a heap of, a mess of, a great deal of, a deal of

entries.meaning: A considerable quantity or number, in Appalachian and Upper South speech.
examples: They paid a right smart of money for that bottom land.
There was a right smart of snow on the ridge road.
"We've got a right smart of work left," he said, looking at the barn.
A right smart of people turned out for the funeral.
She's put up a right smart of beans and tomatoes this summer.
It rained right smart all through the night.
entries.pronunciation note: right here is the intensifying adverb "very" and is unstressed; the phrase carries its main stress on smart
entries.русский: изрядно, порядочно — диал. (Аппалачи и Верхний Юг)
entries.register: regional American — Appalachian and Upper South, chiefly Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, and the Carolinas. Ordinary in older speech there, unknown to most Americans elsewhere, and never written outside dialogue and dialect reporting
entries.goes with: both uncountable nouns (a right smart of money, a right smart of work, a right smart of snow) and plural countable nouns (a right smart of people). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory in the quantifier — ✗ a right smart money. Bare a right smart with no of is the pronoun or the adverb in the same dialects: We got a right smart done today, It rained right smart last night.
entries.pattern: a right smart of [uncountable] · a right smart of [plural countable] · a right smart (adverb: it hurt right smart) · right smart [adjective] (regional: right smart cold)
entries.contrast: Smart here has nothing to do with intelligence: it is the older sense "sharp, brisk, considerable," the one still preserved in a smart pace and in smarting. Right is the regional intensifier "very," the same one in right nice, right quick, and right smart cold. The phrase is one of the most reliable regional markers in American English and outside its home a listener will simply not follow it, which is reason enough to keep it inside quotation marks.
entries.variants: right smart, a right smart bit of, a heap of, a sight of
entries.see also: a mess of, a passel of, a sight of, a power of, a heap of

entries.meaning: A very large quantity of anything, countable or not, in vulgar American slang.
examples: We got a shitload of email about that episode.
There's still a shitload of work left on the second floor.
He spent a crapload of money on a car he drives twice a month.
A buttload of people showed up and we had thirty chairs.
That decision cost the company a shitload of money and two vice presidents.
In the memo version of the same sentence it becomes a great deal of, or at worst a ton of.
entries.pronunciation note: casually /ə ˈʃɪtloʊdə/, "a shitloada"
entries.русский: до хрена, до хренища — груб., обсценное: очень много
entries.register: vulgar slang — obscene, and common in American casual speech among adults who know each other, in comedy, in fiction, and online. Never in: any classroom, any workplace where you are not certain of the room, customer-facing speech, a job interview, a court filing, an academic paper, a business email, or a first conversation with anybody. The softened a crapload of and a buttload of are mildly vulgar rather than obscene and clear some of those bars but none of the formal ones; a boatload of and a truckload of are not vulgar at all and are the safe way to say the same thing
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (a shitload of emails, a shitload of people) and uncountable nouns (a shitload of money, a shitload of work). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a shitload money. The plural shitloads of exists and is equally obscene. It stays before another determiner: a shitload of the paperwork.
entries.pattern: a shitload of [plural countable / uncountable] · shitloads of [noun] · a whole shitload of [noun] · non-vulgar substitutes: a boatload of, a truckload of, a ton of
entries.contrast: The whole family is built on -load, and nothing but register separates its members: a boatload of and a truckload of are neutral, a crapload of and a buttload of are mild, a shitload of is obscene, and all of them take countables and uncountables alike and all of them mean a lot of. Agreement follows the noun after of: A shitload of people were there, A shitload of work is left. If there is any doubt about the room, the sentence works exactly as well with a ton of.
entries.variants: a crapload of, a buttload of, shitloads of, a whole shitload of, a boatload of (not vulgar), a truckload of (not vulgar)
entries.see also: tons of, a heap of, loads of, a lot of, a bunch of

entries.meaning: A great deal of something, countable or not, in older regional American speech.
examples: That fence cost him a sight of money and half a summer.
There was a sight of people at the courthouse that morning.
"You'll save yourself a sight of trouble if you call first," she said.
He knows a sight of things about that river that nobody ever wrote down.
The second doctor was a sight better than the first.
We waited two hours and never got a sight of the parade.
entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /ə/ and the t flaps: /ə ˈsaɪɾə/
entries.русский: страсть сколько, уйма — устар./диал. амер.
entries.register: regional and old-fashioned American — Southern, Appalachian, and older rural New England, and British dialect before that. Alive chiefly in the speech of older speakers; the piece of it most Americans still hear is the adverbial a sight better
entries.goes with: both uncountable nouns (a sight of money, a sight of trouble) and plural countable nouns (a sight of people). Never a bare singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is obligatory in the quantifier — ✗ a sight money. Bare a sight is the commoner survival and is an adverb of degree in front of a comparative: a sight better, a sight more sense, a durn sight worse. That use is not a determiner.
entries.pattern: a sight of [uncountable / plural countable] · a sight [comparative] (adverb: a sight better) · a durn / dang sight [comparative] · compare the ordinary noun in not a sight of him
entries.contrast: Two different things wear this spelling. The quantifier means "a great deal of" and is regional; the ordinary noun means a view or a glimpse, so we never got a sight of him is that noun under a negative and means the opposite of a lot. The adverbial a sight better is the part of the idiom still heard nationally. Its regional neighbors are a power of and a heap of; the neutral equivalent is a great deal of.
entries.variants: a sight better (adverb), a durn sight, a power of, a heap of
entries.see also: a power of, a heap of, a mess of, a right smart of, a great deal of

entries.meaning: A lot of anything, countable or not, in American slang borrowed from French and carried home by the military.
examples: That house out on the point cost beaucoup bucks.
We had beaucoup problems with the first shipment.
He put in beaucoup hours that year and never saw a dime of overtime.
There were beaucoup mosquitoes and not a breath of wind.
"They gave us beaucoup paperwork and about ten minutes to fill it out."
English drops the preposition the French keeps: beaucoup money, never ✗ beaucoup of money.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˌbuˈku/, boo-KOO, which is the pronunciation behind the eye-spellings boocoo and boo-koo; the French original is /boˈku/
entries.русский: море, навалом — амер. сленг из французского, армейского происхождения
entries.position: central and bare — it fills the determiner slot with no article in front of it and no of after it: beaucoup bucks, never ✗ a beaucoup of bucks
entries.register: slang, borrowed from French. It entered American English through servicemen stationed in France and came home again from Vietnam, and it is still strongly associated with the military, with veterans, and with Southern speech. Jocular everywhere else, and not written outside dialogue and casual prose
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (beaucoup problems, beaucoup people) and uncountable nouns (beaucoup money, beaucoup trouble). The commonest collocations are about money — beaucoup bucks, beaucoup dollars. Never a bare singular countable noun: ✗ beaucoup problem.
entries.with of: it takes no of — ✗ beaucoup of money — and no article. This is where the French original and the American slang part company: French beaucoup de requires its preposition, and a speaker who carries it over produces ✗ beaucoup of, which is not the English idiom.
entries.pattern: beaucoup [plural countable] · beaucoup [uncountable] · beaucoup bucks (the stock phrase) · compare French beaucoup de [noun]
entries.contrast: Beaucoup belongs to the small set of American quantifiers that sit bare in the determiner slot with no article and no of — the slang hella and mad and the standard many and much. Register is the thing to get right: in the mouth of a veteran it is unremarkable, in a marketing deck it is a joke, and in a report it is an error. The eye-spellings boocoo and boo-koo are common in American dialogue and are the same word.
entries.variants: boocoo, boo-koo, beaucoup bucks, hella, mad
entries.see also: hella, mad, tons of, a lot of, a shitload of

entries.meaning: A lot of anything, countable or not, in Northern California slang.
examples: There were hella people at Ocean Beach on Saturday.
That parking ticket cost me hella money.
We sat in hella traffic on the bridge for an hour.
She's got hella work due before finals.
My little brother says hecka because our mom won't let him say the other one.
The show was hella good, which is the same word doing the intensifier's job.
entries.pronunciation note: the second syllable is the weak /ə/; there is no /r/ in it
entries.русский: до фига, уйма — сленг Северной Калифорнии; также усилитель «очень»
entries.position: as a quantifier, central and bare — no article, no of: hella people, hella money. As a degree adverb it precedes an adjective or another adverb (hella good, hella fast), which is not a determiner use at all
entries.register: regional American slang — Northern California. It was born in the Bay Area and spread nationally through music and the internet without losing its accent: in the Bay Area it is ordinary casual speech, elsewhere it is either borrowed or performed, and older speakers everywhere hear it as teenage. Not used in writing outside dialogue and social media
entries.type: quantifier, and a degree adverb in its other job
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (hella people, hella cars) and uncountable nouns (hella money, hella traffic, hella work). Never a bare singular countable noun: ✗ hella car.
entries.with of: it takes no of — ✗ hella of people — and no article: ✗ a hella people.
entries.pattern: hella [plural countable] · hella [uncountable] · hella [adjective] (degree adverb: hella tired) · hecka [noun / adjective] (the euphemistic form)
entries.contrast: Hella is a clipping of hell of a, and the clipping is what freed it from the article: a hell of a lot of people collapsed into hella people. It does two jobs and only one of them belongs in this file — before a noun it is a quantifier (hella cars), before an adjective it is an intensifier (hella expensive). The softened hecka is the same word with the profanity filed off and is what gets said in school. Its East Coast counterpart is mad; the neutral equivalent everywhere is a lot of.
entries.variants: hecka, hella (intensifier: hella good), hell of a, mad
entries.see also: mad, beaucoup, tons of, a lot of, a hell of a, one hell of a, one heck of a

entries.meaning: A lot of anything, countable or not, in New York City slang.
examples: There were mad people outside the venue by eight o'clock.
I've got mad respect for what she pulled off with that budget.
He's been putting in mad hours since the promotion.
There's mad traffic on the expressway every afternoon.
The crowd gave the opening act mad love.
Mind the article: mad skills is a great deal of skill, and a mad scientist is something else.
entries.pronunciation note: identical to the ordinary adjective mad; only the grammar tells them apart
entries.русский: немерено, куча — сленг Нью-Йорка: очень много
entries.position: central and bare — no article, no of: mad people, mad respect. It cannot follow a determiner in this sense, and the moment one appears the meaning flips: the mad people is about insanity, not about numbers
entries.register: regional American slang — New York City, out of hip-hop and Black and Latino youth speech of the 1980s and 1990s and spread from there. Still strongly New York-flavored. Casual speech only; nothing about it belongs in writing that is not quoting somebody
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (mad people, mad cars) and uncountable nouns (mad money, mad respect, mad love, mad traffic). Never a bare singular countable noun: ✗ mad car.
entries.with of: it takes no of — ✗ mad of people — and no article: ✗ a mad people.
entries.pattern: mad [plural countable] · mad [uncountable] · mad respect / mad love / mad props (the stock collocations) · mad [adjective] (intensifier: mad cool)
entries.contrast: This is not the adjective. He has mad skills means a great many skills; he has a mad look means something else entirely, and the article is the giveaway, because the quantifier refuses one. Watch the collision with the older national idiom mad money, which means cash set aside for an emergency or a splurge and says nothing about quantity — only context separates the two. Its West Coast counterpart is hella, and like hella it also works as an intensifier before an adjective (mad cool), which is not a determiner use.
entries.variants: mad props, mad respect, mad love, mad (intensifier: mad cool), hella
entries.see also: hella, beaucoup, tons of, a lot of, umpteen

entries.meaning: A collection of people or claims the speaker holds in contempt — archaic, and never neutral.
examples: "We're bought and sold for English gold — such a parcel of rogues in a nation."
The whole defense was a parcel of lies and the jury knew it within an hour.
He called the commissioners a parcel of fools and was removed from the room.
The pamphlet is a parcel of nonsense dressed up in footnotes.
An 1840s witness dismissed the whole claim as a parcel of idle talk.
Today the same insult comes out as a pack of lies.
entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /ə/: /ə ˈpɑrsələ/
entries.русский: свора, сборище — устар. и презр.: a parcel of lies «сплошное враньё»
entries.register: archaic, and wherever it survives, contemptuous. In present-day American English it is alive only in the dismissive frame a parcel of lies, a parcel of fools, a parcel of nonsense, and even there it sounds like a quotation. Its country descendant a passel of is the living form of the same word
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns naming people held in contempt (a parcel of rogues, a parcel of fools, a parcel of idlers) and uncountable nouns naming falsehood or foolishness (a parcel of lies, a parcel of nonsense). It is not used of neutral things: a parcel of chairs reads as the literal noun, a wrapped package of them.
entries.with of: of is obligatory — ✗ a parcel lies. The literal noun is a separate and thoroughly current word — a parcel of land, a parcel from the post office — and there parcel pluralizes freely and carries no scorn.
entries.pattern: a parcel of [rogues / fools / lies / nonsense] · a whole parcel of [noun] · compare literal a parcel of land
entries.contrast: Parcel and passel are one word split in two: the standard spelling kept the contempt, the dialect spelling kept the quantity. Burns fixed the phrase in English with "such a parcel of rogues in a nation," and nearly every modern use is echoing him or the register he wrote in. Where a present-day writer wants the same scorn, the living idiom is a pack of lies — which is exactly what a parcel of lies turned into.
entries.variants: a passel of, a pack of (lies), a whole parcel of
entries.see also: a passel of, a plethora of, a host of, a deal of, a mess of

entries.meaning: The archaic form of enough — a sufficient or plentiful quantity, met today only inside quotation marks.
examples: "A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread — and Thou / Beside me singing in the Wilderness — / Oh, Wilderness were Paradise enow!"
The old ballad promises gold enow to any man who dares the crossing.
He had friends enow while the money lasted.
"There is trouble enow in this house without yours," the housekeeper said.
A nineteenth-century hymn asks whether grace is enow for the day.
Every one of those sentences takes enough in modern English.
entries.pronunciation note: it rhymes with now, not with know, and the first syllable is the weak /ə/ exactly as in enough
entries.русский: устар. форма enough — довольно, вдоволь; встречается только в цитатах
entries.position: before its noun (enow provisions) or, far more often in verse, after it — Paradise enow, gold enow — exactly as enough once could and still can in a few fixed phrases
entries.register: archaic. It is the old northern English and Scots form of enough, dead in American English since the nineteenth century and alive now only in quotation — above all in FitzGerald's Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, which is where nearly every American who knows the word learned it
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (friends enow, books enow) and uncountable nouns (gold enow, trouble enow). Historically enow was the plural-countable form and enough the mass form — books enow beside bread enough — the same countability split that separates many from much; but the distinction had broken down before the word died, and the surviving quotations do not observe it.
entries.with of: in the surviving quotations it takes no of-phrase. Its modern replacement does: enough of the money, enough of them.
entries.pattern: [noun] + enow (postpositive, the usual order in verse) · enow [noun] · compare current enough
entries.contrast: Enow is not a separate word to learn but the ancestor of one: read it as enough every time and the line will make sense. Its historical job — countable plural against mass enough — is the only place in English where sufficiency was ever divided the way many and much divide quantity, and nothing of it survives. Modern American English has no trace of the form at all: write enough.
entries.variants: enough, anow, enow (Scots and northern English)
entries.see also: enough, sufficient, aplenty, ample, plenty of

entries.meaning: A poetic intensification of many a — a great number of things, considered one at a time.
examples: "Full many a gem of purest ray serene / The dark unfathom'd caves of ocean bear."
"Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air."
The hymn recalls full many a year of wandering before the promise was kept.
Full many an evening had ended the same way in that house.
Full many a traveler had turned back at the pass, and the guide could name them all.
Strip the old adverb off and the living phrase remains: many a traveler turned back.
entries.pronunciation note: full here has the vowel of pull, /fʊl/, and is unstressed; the phrase carries its stress on many, and the article stays the weak /ə/
entries.русский: устар., поэт. усиление many a — «весьма многие», по одному
entries.position: predeterminer — the article a is locked inside the phrase, so nothing may precede it: ✗ the full many a gem
entries.register: archaic and poetic. It is a verse intensification of many a, at home in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century English poetry, and the line most Americans have met it in is Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard. No living register produces it
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only, exactly as many a does — full many a gem, full many a flower, full many a time. Never a plural (✗ full many a gems) and never an uncountable noun. The singular runs through the whole clause: Full many a flower is born to blush unseen.
entries.with of: it never takes of — ✗ full many a of them. Before a vowel sound the article changes as usual: full many an hour.
entries.pattern: full many a [singular countable] + singular verb · full many an [vowel-initial singular noun]
entries.contrast: Full here is the old adverb meaning "very," the same one preserved in full well (you know full well) and in the archaic full sore; it is not the adjective, and it never agrees with anything. Strip it off and what remains is plain many a, which is formal but alive. Its companion intensification is many and many a, which repeats rather than amplifies. Both belong to verse, and in modern prose both read as pastiche.
entries.variants: many a, many and many a, full well (the surviving adverb)
entries.see also: many a, many and many a, many's the, many, enow

entries.meaning: An emphatic, repeated many a — a great many occasions, one after another, in a storytelling voice.
examples: "It was many and many a year ago, / In a kingdom by the sea."
Many and many a night he sat up with the lamp burning.
The old woman had told that story many and many a time.
Many and many an hour was lost at that crossing before the bridge went in.
Many and many a traveler passed that way and left nothing behind.
In plain modern English the sentence says simply many nights.
entries.pronunciation note: the linking and is always the weak /ən/ or a bare /n/, never the full /ænd/; the second many carries the main stress
entries.русский: устар., лит.: «много-много раз» — эмфатический повтор many a
entries.position: predeterminer, with the article a locked inside the phrase — nothing may precede it
entries.register: archaic and literary; a reduplication used in nineteenth-century verse and storytelling for emphasis and rhythm. Poe's "It was many and many a year ago, / In a kingdom by the sea" is the line that keeps it in circulation. Living speakers produce it only in a deliberately storybook voice
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only — many and many a year, many and many a time, many and many a night — with a strong preference for nouns of time. Plural and uncountable nouns are both impossible: ✗ many and many a years, ✗ many and many a money. Singular agreement runs through the clause.
entries.with of: it never takes of — ✗ many and many a of them. Before a vowel sound the article changes: many and many an hour.
entries.pattern: many and many a [singular countable, usually a time word] + singular verb · many and many an [vowel-initial noun] · compare plain many a and intensified full many a
entries.contrast: The three members of the family differ only in weight. Many a night is formal but current; full many a night is poetic and amplified; many and many a night is poetic and repeated, and the repetition does as much work for "again and again" as for "a great number." It is the most sing-song of the three and the least usable in prose. The doubling is the same pattern behind again and again and round and round.
entries.variants: many a, full many a, many and many a time, many's the
entries.see also: many a, full many a, many's the, many, umpteen

entries.meaning: There have been a great many occasions of the kind named — a fronted, reminiscent way of saying many a.
examples: Many's the night I fell asleep at that desk.
Many's the time she warned him about that road in the winter.
Many's the man who has lost a boat in that channel.
Many's the story that came out of the mill and never made the paper.
Many's the dollar the two of them spent trying to keep it running.
The ordinary version is flatter and says the same thing: many a night I fell asleep there.
entries.pronunciation note: the contracted 's is /z/ and the article is the weak /ðə/, becoming /ði/ only before a vowel
entries.русский: сколько раз бывало… — разг.-старомодный зачин о множестве случаев
entries.position: predeterminer inside a fronted noun phrase: the phrase opens the sentence and a relative clause completes it — Many's the night I fell asleep at that desk. It cannot appear anywhere else in the sentence
entries.register: old-fashioned but not dead — still produced by living American speakers reaching for a folksy, reminiscent tone, and common in older fiction and in Irish and Irish-American speech. It is the one form in this section you might actually hear said out loud
entries.type: quantifier in a fixed clause frame
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only — many's the night, many's the time, many's the man, many's the story — with nouns of time dominating. Never a plural (✗ many's the nights) and never an uncountable noun.
entries.with of: it never takes of. The frame instead requires a clause: many's the + singular noun + a relative clause, with the relative pronoun usually left out — Many's the time I have wondered rather than Many's the time that I have wondered.
entries.pattern: many's the [singular countable] + [relative clause] · many's the man who … · many's the time [subject + verb] · compare many a [singular noun] in ordinary subject position
entries.contrast: The frame is an inversion. It means there have been many nights when …, with the quantity pushed to the front as a predicate, and that is why the sentence cannot continue as an ordinary clause: ✗ Many's the night was cold is wrong, because many's the night is not the subject of what follows. Plain many a night is an ordinary subject (Many a night was cold) and can sit anywhere in the sentence, where many's the can only open one.
entries.variants: many a, many's the time, many's the man, many and many a
entries.see also: many a, many, full many a, many and many a, a good many

entries.meaning: Names the largest share of a vote or a group — and, in patent drafting, nothing grander than "more than one."
examples: She won a plurality of the vote in a five-way primary and never came near fifty percent.
A plurality of the members favored postponement, but the bylaws require a majority.
Under state law the office goes to whoever takes a plurality of the votes cast.
The claim recites a housing comprising a plurality of vents.
A plurality of respondents named cost as the main obstacle; no single answer drew half.
A plurality is not a majority, and a plurality of forty-two percent is the usual reason for a runoff.

body: In elections and in any counted body, the largest share, whether or not it passes half — a plurality of the vote. 2. In United States patent claims, exactly "two or more" and no more than that — a plurality of vents.
examples: She won a plurality of the vote in a five-way primary and never came near fifty percent.
A plurality of the members favored postponement, but the bylaws require a majority.
Under state law the office goes to whoever takes a plurality of the votes cast.
The claim recites a housing comprising a plurality of vents.
A plurality of respondents named cost as the main obstacle; no single answer drew half.
A plurality is not a majority, and a plurality of forty-two percent is the usual reason for a runoff.

entries.pronunciation note: the t flaps to /ɾ/ in American speech, as it does in majority and variety
entries.русский: относительное большинство голосов — юр./полит.; в патентах «более одного»
entries.register: technical — election law and political reporting in the first sense, patent drafting in the second. Outside those two worlds an American meets it on election night and nowhere else
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a plurality of voters, a plurality of the votes cast, a plurality of the members. In patent claims it takes any countable noun at all: a plurality of apertures. Never an uncountable noun: ✗ a plurality of money.
